A HAPPY HEART. A happy heart that goeth all day, _ Nor fails in the heat of the noon, It cheerily plods on the long winding way, Where sad hearts grow weary so soon. AVaeart that is happy and gay, The sadness of life can beguile;. 4 beareth the burden and heat of the day, And meeteth each frown with a- smile. Oh, hearts that are happy and glad, Ye leaven earth's sorrow and pain-6._ And ye shall be blest by the weary andisad Ye bring back to brightness again. A happy heart goeth all day, A sunbeam, unquenched by the showers, It heedeth no thorn-branch besetting the way, But findeth delight in the flowers. A heart that is happy and gay, With sweetness and light can illume The lives that go sunless and sad on their way, And fill them with beauty and bloom. Oh, hearts that are happy and glad, Ye leaven earth's sorrow and pain, And ye shall be blest by the weary and sad Ye win back to brightness again. ...Helen Marion Burnside in Girl's then Paper.

THE LIFEBOAT. With threat'aing frown the sun sinks down, An leaves a lurid sky; The cloudy rack drives swift and black, The winds rise loud and high. The mother hears the rising storm— Her heart is sick and sad; Her thoughts go out upon the sea To her dear sailor-lad. The wife looks out into the night, And closer hugs her child, Whose father's ship perchance is tossed • By winds and waters wild. The night wears wearily away, Yet loud the tempest raves. Hark! through the gloom a cannon's boom Is swept across the waves! Again! again! that note of dread Is heard above the roar., See! light on light is flashing bright Along the surf-beat shore. Hurrah! she's launched! with:many a cheer The lifeboat sweeps away, Breasting the mighty swell that rolls And thunders up the bay. The first red ray of dawning day Is gleaming o'er the sea, A noble vessel shoreward drives, The black cliffs on her lee. Now do your best, ye gallant men! Bend bravely to the oar, - Ye yet shall bring that vessel's crew In safety to the shore. 'Tis done! the lifeboat's bows are turned; Swiftly it nears the land. Ho! every man upon the beach, Be sharp and lend a hand ! The well-flung rope uncoils, and falls ' Upon the sandy beach. And quickly is the lifeboat run Beyond the surges' reach. And cottage fires blaze high snd bright, • And cottage cheer is free, To all the lifeboat's gallant crew Saved fro.rn the stormy sea. All honour to our lifeboat crews, And proudly may we boast The deeds of daring they have done Along our rocky coast. R. P. S

The question of the hour—" What time is it?" The injury of prodigality leads to this—that he who will not economise will have to agonise. Fear to do base, unworthy things, is valour. _a they be done to us, to suffer them is valour too. A wise man prefers what is necessary to that which serves only for curiosity, ornament, or pleasure. A man would never be too confident of anything if he always remembered how often he had been mistaken. "Loving kindness," says the Talmud, "is greater than laws; and the charities of life are more than all cere- monies."

REASON Pau SILENCE.—Someone asked Fontaine,/ the celebrated geometrician, what he did in society where he remained almost perfectly silent. "I study,' replied he, "the vanity of men, in order to mortify it occasion- ally." How SHE MANAGED.—" How do I manage to rid my- self of bores ?" said a woman of the world. "Nothing . easier. When I want to send a man away, I talk to him about myself. When I want him to stay indefinitely, I talk about himself." It is the part of a wise and of a good man to deal:with his inferior as he would have his superior deal with him. He that duly •considers how many servants have come to be masters, and how many masters to be ser- va.nts, will lay no great stress upon the one title or upon the other.

A deaf and dumb girl was once asked bya lady, who wrote the question on a slate, "What is prayer.?" The little girl took the pencil and wrote the reply, • Prayer is the wish of the heart." So it is. Fine words and beau- tiful verses said to God do not make real prayer with- out the sincerest wish of the heart. _

An Irish gentleman, in the warmth of national venera- tion, was praising Ireland for the cheapness of provi- sions; salmon might be bought for sixpence, and a dozen mackerel for twopence. "And pray, sir, how came you -to leave so cheap a country ?" "Arrah, honey! where were the sixpences and twopences to be got 7' Small virtues require the praise of men to sustain -them, just as little children require encouragement to walk or stand alone. But true virtue goes quietly through the world, scattering good around, and perform- ing noble deeds without even the knowledge that what it does is heroic:

It is a vulgar notion that politeness is only required towards superiors. But-the truth is that every man ought to regard his fellow man, or friend, as his supe- rior, and treat him accordingly. Such feelings the real gentleman always has. "Let each esteem others better -thaxi himself," says an Apostle. This is tbe very soul of good manners. I have been more and-more convinced, the more I think of it, that, in general, pride is at the bottom of all great mistakes. All the other passions do occasional good; but whenever pride puts in its word everything goes wrong; and whatever it might be desirable to do quietly and innocently, it is mortally dangerous to do proudly.—Ruskin. SHAKESPEARE S Wirx.—Any person desirous of inspect- ing the actual last Will and Testament of the immortal bard of Avon can, do an by visiting Somerset House and pay- ing a shilling. The visitor is conducted to a dimly-lighted room in which this precious relic is praserved, and is not a little astonished to find it secur4v fixed in a series of frames protected by glass. The WM remained for many years without .any attempt being made te protect it from the wear to which it wis subjected. Indeed, the reference to the Will during the period at which it was unprotected has slightly worn away the writing at the folds of the paper. It is a remarkable ‘fact that for every Englishman who visits Somerset House to inspect it, ,there are at least two Americans. The Will has been reproduced in fac- simile on two or three acc.asions at distant intervals, one of the last copies taken being in 1864, when a fac-simile (now out of print) was published at six shillings. Fac-similee have for many years. past been exceedingly scarce, and a sovereign or more has been paid for good copies. Messrs. Cas- -sell and Company have now reproduced the Will in a form which will enable eyery person to possess it, for they have tweed a fac-simile copy with Part 1 of ," Cassell's Illus- trated Shakespeare," the price of the Part, incldding the Will, being but 7d. This new he-simile of the Will has been very carefully executed, its permanent value being greatly enhanced by its being printed on paper of antique style, and in ink similar in colour to that of the original -document.

I THE WORLD IN A bROP OF Wavra,—The microscope • has-shown that.a drop of water, though it may appear , to the naked eye to be perfectly clear, is swarming with living beings. According to. Ehrenberg, a cubicinch of , water may contain more than 800,000 millions 61 these j beings, estimating them only to occupy one-fourth of its space; and a single drop, placed under. the microscope, i will be Seen' to hold 500 millions, an amount, Perhaps, not so very far from equal to the whole number of human beings on the surface of our globe! , What great philanthropy does-the man Of leisure work out ;or the benefit of his brother men? The hard.-W-Ork- i ing man, the studious and professional man whose every hour represents work, are the pillars of the social and commercial worlds. The man of leisure may be orna- mental, may be a pecuniary acquisition in some phases " of social life; but the man who helps to bear the bur- dens of the day, and builds up a h6me, is not the man of leisure. That period of life sometimes comes to the 'working man, and he it is who knows how to utilise it• . to the best advantage. MINUTE SCREIVS.—A newspaper correspondent de- scribes the American watch manufactory at Waltham, Mass., and in speaking of the-astonishing minuteness of some very essential parts of the watch, says :—" A small heap of grain was shown to us, looking like iron filings or grains of pepper from a pepper caster—apparently the mere dust of the machine which turned them out,— and these, when examined with a microscope, were seen 4 to be perfect screws, each to be driven to its .place with sorew-driver. It is one of the statistics at Waltham worth remembering, that a single pound ot steel, cost- ing but 50 cents, is thus •manufactured into 100,000 screws, which are worth S 11." . MAKING RAZOR BrAuts.—Razor blades are forged from cast steel, and are ground and. scorched to take off the black scale, being heated in a coke or charcoal fire and dipped obliquely into water. 'After being drilled and stamped they are hardened and tempered. In tempering, they are laid on their backs on a clear fire and are re- moved as their edges attain a pale straw colour. Shavings of leather added to the fire prevent cracking when the blades are put into water. After tempering they are ground successively on stone, a lap charge with fine emery, and a second lap with -finer emery:-The final polish is given on a soft leather wheel charged with crocus, both razor and wheel being heated. ,It is then honed, working from the point to the heel, being laid flat for the purpose. Wire edges are rubbed off on a ' horn.

THE ROYAL LIVER Socmr.—punch contains the fol- lowing information respecting the Royal Myer Society: —ln answer to numerous correspondents who have seen, this heading, but are too busy to study the reports in the papers, we beg to explain that the object and raison d'etre of this society are, as- evidenced in its title, the preservation of the Royal Constitution. The presidents are her Gracious Majesty and HAIL the Prince of Wales. The consulting medical men belong to the Royal Household, assisted by Dr. Quain, with power to add to their number. There is a yearly subscription, and for this every member is entitled to a certain number of Podophyllin pills and other liver prescriptions, signed by the,committee. The rules of the society enn daily exercise on- horseback, if possible, if not on'' 'foot or gymnastic. The mounted members of the Liver Society may choose their own hours tor horse exercise in the Park, or where they will. When H.R.H. the president takes his regulation ride in the Row, all the members of the Liver Society are expected to be present, Nttguded by their livery servants. Thoseilnembers who hate no stables of their own are bound to use livery stable's. For further particulars, ask anybody. THE AUTOMATIC COUPLER.—" Augustus, dear:' said Mildred, as she seated herself at a distance from him of five-eighths of an inch last night, "Amy asked me to- day what these.new automatic couplers were mentioned in the papers, and I told her that in all probability they were attachments to the new married license law. Are my darling," replied Augustus, "they wthoeryk?ed" the new wautomatic coupler for the first time at Waynesburg on Tuesday, and it" acted like, a charm." "Tell me about it, dear." "Well, the couple went to.the- Clerk of Court, got a license called' in 'some witnesses, and the man said, We acknowledge each ether to be husband and wife,' and the automatic coupler had done its deadly work." "0, dear! is that the way- it operates ? and Mildred looked very disconsolate. "Yes, shall we do it in that way, dear ?" "If that is the new style I suppose we'll have to, but I don't like it. Can't we have it some other-way?" "Oh, certainly! Thi4, when 'the heat in I the egg drawer, above which it is plaood, reaches that ' point, the expansion of this capsule is made to move a lever, which in its turn acts u'pon a cap above the latiip. By this arrangement, which,itis unncessary to explain more .fully here, An ' equable temperature is main- tairTea, and, as already ' stated, its regularity is very remarkable. We nave been very pleased in- deed with the provision made for the supply qf fresh air- and moisture, Wci say provision becausb .one is really part of the other. - The bottom of the egg drawer is made of perforated zinc, covered with coarse canvas, so that air will pass through freely:, Below this drawer is a square tin tray, in the centre ot.;which is a low capped shaft. This tray less then inverted over it another tray made of perforated zinc, with half- inch holes. Above this is laid another piece of coarse 'canvas, and when the ends are tucked down into the larger tray, which is filled with water, the capillary action keeps the whole of the canvas moist. In what is the bottom of the machine is a large air hole. As this is the only inlet for the air, and the shaft of the 'water tray is iramediately above, it. will be seen that ere the current of fresh air can find its way to the egg' drawer, it 'must pass through the damp canvas. 'Therei it is moistened and becomes charged'with as much water as it can carry. This appears to us the perfection of cora- munication.of moisture to-the eggs. The ventilation is also effeetiyely secured, as the fresh, air passes up as freely as it can circulate up and around the eggs, and i passes out Of the machine-by holes plaoed level with the 'bottom of the water tank. There is another advantage ' derived from this systein of ventilation, namely,?that the bottoms of the eggs ,are kept cooler than the tops. Mr. Henry Boyle, by his experiments some years ago, showed this to be the natural condition-of eggs under hens. We have made some tests to see the temperature of the air as it travels through the machine. This'showecrus that when the temperature of the air in the room was 58degs., and consequently the same as it entered the machine, as it passed through the water tray it roae to 72clegs.;'when , it reached the bottom of the eggs it was•9sdegs., -and above the eggs 104degs. This experiment shoirs that there is no clanger with this,system of ventilation of. a chilling of the eggs, through a suddert rush' in of cold air. It also shows that the ventilating and supilly of fresh airto the eggs needs no interference from or will, cause thought to the worker of the machine. AA THE ROYAL" SHOW OF 1886. . It will be remembered that last year the Rciyal Agricultural Society of England added poultry to the show held then at Preston, and that a large measure of success attended the venture. We are glad- to see that this feature of the show is to be continued at the Nor- wich meeting in July next, for which the schedule has just been issued. Ws is usual with whatever is done by the Royal Society the prizes offered are very liberal in- deed, and we hope that the response will be much greater than was the case last year, good though that was; but it is not often the case that on the , first ven- ture a full measure of success is obtained,' especially when the system adopted is so thoroughly out of the ordinary ruts, as was the fact- in this instance, Instead of the single bird Or pair system being adopted, it will be remembered that each entry Oonsisted Of a cock and three hens, except in the gSme section, where separate classes were provided for cocks, the same. number of hens ht.tvizig to be shown as in the other classes. - This is, in 'short, the French system. We expressed our views upon it last year and it is unnecessary to repeat them now. The same plan is to be followed at the Nor- ,-wich show, and-also that of giving classes for chickens of the year, as well as for adult birds. Thus whilst the number of breeds or varieties `represented,in this schedule are 244 there are 48 classes. In each class are to be given three prizes, namely, first, £3; second, ..£2 ; and third, £l. The total amount offered is therefore nearly £3OO, and as the entry fee for each pen is only ss. for non-members of the society, and 2s. 6d. for mom- vipers, it will be seen that the prizes are very liberal in- deed, much more so 'than is generally the case at agri- I'cultural shows.
A.

There are few changes in the classes from the show of last year, two breeds having been omitted, namely, .Spanish and Polish, but their places are taken by what must be regarded as more useful varieties—Scotch Greys and linorcas. The schedule in one respect is remark- able, for, with the exception of Cochins, there is now no ,breed included but what is strong in economic qualities. Even Cochins, when properly crossed, may be made use- ful in the impartation of their winter laying qualities. From the position taken up by the Royal Agricultural 'Society, that rs, to 'make the poultry section of their show of practical importance to farmers and agricul-- tural labourers, it is very desirable that mere fancy breed's should be excluded. Whilst perhaps some minor alterations could be suggested, so far as the classification is concerned, it will be difficult to improve the schedule. Perhaps in a year or two, if Wyandottes. go on griming in popularity, they may be added, and it might be desir- able to give classes for the little known, but valuable, Sussex fowl, and to divide the colours of geese. The following are the breeds provided for, and the number of classes given to each t.—Brahmas 4, Cochins 2, Lang- slims 2, Houdans 2, Plymouth Rocks 2, Scotch.Grevs 2, Andalusians 2, Minorcas 2, Hamburghs 4, Legherits 2, Dorkings 6, Creves 2, • Game 4, Ducks 8, Geese 2, and Turkeys 4. We wish that the society could see its way to include some classes for first crosses, and also for table poultry, both pure and cross-bred. If the system adopted at Birmingham and the dairy shows could be carried out, that is, having the birds shown alive first, and then killed, it would ava means of education which cannot be equalled in any other way. This, we hope, may yet come. The rules of the show do not require any special notice from us, as intending exhibitors can obtain copies of the schedule froni the secretary of the society, H. M. Jenkins, Esq., 12, Hanover-square, London, W. The dates upon which the show is to be held are July 12th, and four following days, and the entries in the Poultry section close on June Ist.

WIFE Munnian.—At the Staffordshire Assizes, on Thurs- day, john Davies, 54, pa tern maker, was sentenced to death for the murder of his wife at Wolverhampton on the sth November. The prisoner and the &ceased hal been living apart, and on the woman refusing to live with him again the prieoner beat her to death with a poker in a schoolroom where she was employed as cleaner. THE Piratic° MYSTERY.—The coroner's inquiry into the circumstances attending the dpath of Mr. Bartlett, of Pim- lico, London, was resumed on Monday. Mr. Ardwick, chemist, Pimlico, banded in copies of the prescriptions made up for the deceased since December 10th. Mr. Dyson (Wesleyan minister) was recalled, and, replying to Mr. Dennis (who watched the case for the relatives of the de- ceased), said he was often in the house alone with Mee. Bartlett. When they were at Dover Mrs. Bartlett asked him to correspond with her. He did so daily, but had destroyed the letters. He admitted that he told an untruth to procure the chloroform, but believed it was for a proper use. He could not sly whether he should have mentioned these matters bad there been no post-mortem. He mentioned the matter after that because he suspected the chloroform had been put to a criminal use. That was why he told Mrs. Bart- lett he had been duped. He threw away the bottles in which the chlOroform had been purchased. The inquiry, so far as concerned Mrs. Bartlett, having closed, evidenee was called by Mr. Lickfold .in support of Mr. Dyson's statement. The Rev. Mr. Riegel, of Goole, and Mrs. Matth?we deposed to Mr. Dyson having made to them explanatione similar to those made by him at the in- quest, end Mr. Matthews testified to Mr. Dysoe's groat die- tress at what had occurred. The inquiry was further ad- journed, Mr. Dyson entering into recognisances to appear at the adjourned hearing. On Thursday the coroner's in- quiry as to the death of Mr. Bartlett in Pimlico was can. eluded. In reading over the evidence of the witnesses the ICoroner pointed out that the Rey. Mr. Dyson had said nothing about the purchase of chloroform until after the first sitting of the jury. The jury, he supposed, were agreed that Mrs. Bartlett should be committed for wilful murder by the action they took a week ago. The evidence since given had not altered the case as against her, and the main question was how far Mr. Dyson, who bought the chloroform, was an accessory before the fact. He left it to them to say if they were satisfied with Mr. Dyson's ex- planation. The jury retired at ten minutes after five, and returned into court with a verdict of " Wilful murder " against both Mrs. Bartlett and Mr. Dyson. The Coroner , made Oct a warrant for the apprehension of Mr. Dyson, who was arrested at once. He turned deadly pale and wept, and was removed to Westminster Police Station, adjoining ' the police court, where he will next appear in the dock with ( Mrs. Bartlett. It is stated that Mrs. Bartlett has since her arrest made a statement somewhat contradictory to that of ' Mr. Dyson.

MURDER ST A BOY.—At Liverpool Assiss?s. on Monday, before Mr. Justice Day, Michael Lavelle, 16, a sawyer's as- sistant, was indicted for the murder.at Liverpool, on the let inst., of Maxwell Kirkpatrick. Deceased, who was 42 years of age, was just before his death workimg in a timber yard in Byrom-street, Liverpool, and had previously word at the timber vard of Mr. Tickle. The prisoner had also worked at the latter place with the deceased, and they appear to have had frequent quarrels, produced, according to the defence, by the bullying conduct of the deceased. The de- , ceased had called the prisoner an "Irish nig," and that an- noyed the prisoner, who threw a roller at the deceased, and was afterwaids heard to say that be would take his life. On the afternoon of the day in question deceased was going home, and when in Everton Brow the deceased came up be- hind, and, calling out "Hallo, Mac," struck him a blow .on the head with a wooden roller. The deceased fell on the ground, and when picked up was able, with assistance, to reach home. THE ENGLISH IN BURMAH. MAliperea.Y, SkTURDA.I.—An influential deputation of foreign residents in Mandalay presented an address to Lord Dufferin, in which the following passage occurs :—" We re- joice to receive you as the representative of the Queen Em- Press as Viceroy of India, as a statesman who has made himself beloved in every country over which he has ruled, and who has always increased the happiness and welfare of those he has governed. In Upper Burteah there exists a Wide ,field of improvement by developing the vast but hither° neglected resources of the country, by restorieg Peace and order, by confirming to all a just and impartial ad-ministration of the law, and by securing to the people all those blessings which flow from English rule."—Although no official declaration has been made, it may with some tonfidence be stated that both Upper and Lower Burmah 'VI he united into one province, under the government of reßernard. The administration will be carried on by Bnglish officials, but all minor posts will be filled by Bur- raese. It has been decided to unite the military commands of both provinces under General Prendergast, assisted by brigadiers. • IteleGOON, MONDAy.---Lord Dtaffarin has lost tee time in arriving at a decision in regard to the future government of Upper Emmett. After a carefel consideration of the facts submitted to him, aided by the knowledge gained by per- sonal observation and inquiry, he has decided that the n9untry is not yet ripe for the establishment of a system of wv"il administration and law. The military occupation .rel martial law will therefere continue as at present twill 4vereber next. The garrison will consist cif 16,000 men— and Indian troops—under the supreme command of ,zeneral Prenchrgast. The Viceroy lass ale° recognised the rh,,et'sairY of ;promptly -enforcing British authority in the el-entry, whither a strong expeditionary force Will be despatched with the least possible delay. The following gentlemen will assist Mr. Childers in his inquiry into the conduct of the police with regard to the London disturbance: Lord Wolselev, Lord Edward Caveudisb, M.P., Sir H. Holland, M.P.' and Mr. C. T. Ritchie, M.P.—Summonses were granted by Sir J. Ingham, at Bow-street on Saturday afternoon against Messrs. Hynd- man Champion, Burns, and Williams, for having on the previous Monday delivered seditious speeches inciting to a breach of the peace. At the Marlborough-street Police Court, on Saturday, a number of tradesmen and others resid- ing in the west end of the metropolis waited by arrange- meat upon Mr. Mansfield, the presiding magistrate, to press their claims against the county for the losses they sus- tained during the riots. About 200 claims have been made out, amounting in the aggregate to £llOOO. London work- ing-men have formally repudiated any connection with Messrs. Hyndman, Champion, Burns, and the "wealthy leaders of the Democratic Federation" generally. At a meeting on Clerkenwell-green on Sunday morning, under the presidency of Mr. P. Kenny, of the Amalgamated Labourers' Union, the Democratic Federation was de- nounced, and its leaders described as "the teimitigated enemies of the werking classes, who, without the authority of any bona fide working-men's organisation, led on the sweepings of the metropolis' the scum of society, to plunder West-end shops." At the Guild-hall Police Court, London, on Monday, two men were sentenced to two months' hard labeur and another to one month's imprisctment for par- ticipating in the riots. It is stated that the Socialist defen- dants will subpenna a number of members of the Govern- ment to justify the language 'for which they are prosecuted. The following communication has been 'forwarded to Mr. eladstone :—" Palate Chambers, Feb. leltb. Messrs. Burns, Champion, Ilyndman, Hunter, Watts, and Williams having ^received no answer to their memorial of Friday to the 1 Prime Minister, now enclose a series of.peeposals for dealing! with distress published by the Social Democratic Fedora- tion more than two years ago. That the distress, even then I great, is now still more -carious, can ma longer be denied. Messrs. Burns, Chempion, Hyndanaa, Hunter, Watts, and! Williams press the Prime Minister, therefore, on behaltd: 1 the unemployed, for at immedhte -answer to their letter.l The Social temocretic 7ederation have summoned a meet- ing in Hyde Park on Sunday nextleeb. 21st, to demand in an orderly kit determined manner that tho executhe should nodal:ger refese to organise the labour of those who are now starving through no fault of their own. To-this meeting Messrs. B-ar' ns Champion, Hyndman, Roster, Wears; and Williams will be glad to state that the Govern- ment have relolved to follow the precedent set in other periods of-distress by at once commencing useful public works (not criminai tasks), and paying to those engaged rates of wages stancient to ensure a healthy snlesistence.." Thetemmittee of inquiry formed by the Home Secretary to investigate the conduct of 'the police during the riets in London -met on Tuesday afternoon and sat for three hours and a half. Mr. Childers presided. The police commis- sioners-and superintendents] were examined. On Wednesday, Messrs. H. Hyndmana, John Burns, H. , Champion, and Jam E. 'Williams appeared at Bow-street 'Police Court, to answer -summonses connected with the I 'riots last Monday week,. Mr. Poland opened the prosecu- tion, and said the charge was sedition by means of violent and inflammatory speeches tending to provoke a breach of the peace. He then related the occurrence on the occasion , of the riots, and the part taken by the defendants, as he r wcuid show daring the investigation. Mr. John White, al reporter for the Times, said he attended the meeting on I Monday, the Bth, in 'Trafalgar Square. The defendant Burns was there, and one person with a'red flag stood at j the corner of Nelson's 'Column. Burns eaid "Unless the ; people have bread others must have lead:" He repeated tlria twice. Witness 'had destroyed his shorthand notes, I -and said this from memory. The four defendants were ,1 , there, and delivered ppeeches, Burns being the chairman. He eonki swear that Ilyndman said, " If:the thousandil there had the courage they would soon alter the existirtg state of things." Mr. Rendle, reporter of the 'Daily !Tele- -74k-said Barns and Williams were at the demonstration. • Burne said, "The neret time we come here it will be to sack the bakers' shops in the West End." He corroborated 1 'Mr. White as to the other expressions used by Burns. 'ilefr. Haling, another Daily l'elograh reporter, ssid he ; followed the crowd to Hyde Park. A red flag was waved 1 in •Trafalgar Square and Pall Mall. ff.e saw windows broken in St. Jarnees-street and Piccadilly, and carratges ,attacked. 1 A meeting of the unemployed of Birmingham was held on i Monday, on Gosta•Green. Close upon 10,000 people-were I present, who were harangued by some men who have identi- r.led themselves with.the unempfoyed movement. At first the preceedings were of an orderly character, and the vast audience contented themselves with applauding vociferously i any remarks (aed many were made) which in any degree I denounced the Town Council and the Board ef Guardians; : buttetter the passing of a resolution calling upon the •Mayor I to, convene a townEs meeting, and deciding to adjourn the meeting until Thursday to await hie answer, the crowd be came unruly. At this point a ,violent speech was made by a Mr. Hopkins, who grew 'very excited. He shouted :—" I cootend that you should act•staree. Do your duty like men, and stand together. It is better for you to fight for bread, and to die in fighting, than to die by starva- tion. -(Loud cheers.) Be men, and dolee be cowards. -Fight for what you require. (Cheers.) • Yon are entitled to march through the town of Birmingham and show your distress. You are entitled to ' do alio, and I contend that there is not a zeldier that dares ' nnebeath his sword until the Riot Act is read. (Vocifer- ousubeering.) We'll eneetio the Bull Bing on Thursday ! night, and see what can be done." (Applause.) This -speech had its effect, the crowd grew more _unruly, and made a rush for the platform, while the Rev. Dr. Gardiner appealed for quietude and order, and abstention from riot. The Chairman hastily annoacced the meeting at an end, and the speakers hastily retreated from their dangerous position. Scenes of violence and excitement were witnessed in tiseetreets through velaich,the crowd wended their-way. A number of rorghs who got in the market showed a dizpo- sition to loot the stalls, Out the firm attitude of the stall- keepers prevented this. Gem • fishmonger had his watch cello. The shopkeepers in the bottom part of New-street and neighbourhood, and those in the Bull Ring, pat their shutters tap; but many of the balconies over the shops and upper windows were filled with -spectators who appeared no look upon the whole proceedings as great fun. Time after time the mounted police scattered everything before them, but the crowd re-formed each time. At length the foot police were formed into cordons, and they swept the streets either way. As a result the, mob was gradually broken up into several detachments, the largest of which proceeded along Neat-street, and came tea-halt at the corner of Stephenson-place. They were followed by the police, whose persistent attempts to effect a complete dispersal were crowned with euccess before a quarter past two. The two banks in New-street were closed between one and two' o'clock in the afternoon, and preperations were made to withstand any attack which might he made upon the build- i ings. Although Lloyd's bank in High-street was not cloud, l the whole of theclerks were armed with loaded revolvers. The propesed march to Mr. Chateberlain'e house fell through altogether, and so adroitly were the police man- aged, and so promptly was any attempt to forma procession dealt with by the übiquitous mouoted police, that the mob was practically powerless. DEA.TH .OF MR. J. B. GOUGH. PHILADELPHIA., TuEspl_a.—Mr.'John B. Gough,,the well- known lecturer, had a fatal stroke of paralysis while lecturing O n temperance at the Frankford Presbyterian Church, Phila- '.lelphia, last night. His a A ge was sixty-eight. ,Ir...Gongh b4s delivered nearly nine thousand lectures aurtag his oireer.

John B. Gough was borne at Sandgao, Kent, Augnet 22, 1817. 41:n 1829 he emigratedto New Ycrk, learned the trade of a bookbinder, and fell into habits of intemperance. In 9ctober, 1842, he was induced to attend a temperance meet- • Mg. Here he took the pledge of abstinence, and soon began Publicly to advocate the principle. His reputation as an 'orator spread through the United States and Canada and reached England. In 1853 the London Temperance League -invited him to visit Great Britain. The visit, intended to ,last only six weeks, was protracted to two yeare;during which he advocated the cause of temperance thronghout the •island. He then resumed his labours in America. In 1857 he again came to England, and lectured with still greater •ncc-ss until 1860, when he returned to America. He now began to lecture on other topics with great success, acquir- a large income. In 1846 he published his " Autobio- graphy ;" a volume of "Orations" in 1854; a collection Of " Temperanoc Lectures" in 1879 ; and "Sunlight and Shadow, or Gleanings from my Life-Work," in 1880. In 1873 he announced that he was about to leave the field as a .üblic lecturer; but he suboequently appeared at intervals. !In 1878 he again alsited England.—ea of the Time.

verting to Ireland, he remarked that the Tories for a long time had been asserting that the Liberal party meant to do something that shall endanger the integrity of the empire. But he wished them to remember that before 1800 there was a Parliament in Dublin, and that the British Empire never- theless existed. He believed that a Parliament could be re- ' establlsbed in Dublin, and that the British Empire would not tumble to pieces en that account. He asked them to remember that there were eighty-five determined representa- tives of Ireland sitting on the Opposition side, and if they were not satisfied 'no good work could be done for England. Because he loved Ireland and believed that she was entitled to self-government, because he loved England still more and de- sired the accomplishment of the great reforms in the Liberal programme, and because he was firmly convinced that the integrity of the empire would be maintained after the estab- lishment of Home Rule, he was ready to support the measures contemplated by Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues. (Loud applause) A vote 'of thanks to the chairman closed the proceed- ings.

COUNCIL. ANNUAL MEETING.

- The atunal meeting of the Council of the li`orth- wich Division Liberal Association was held in the Drill Hall, Northwich, on Saturday. There was a good attendance of delegates from all parts of the division, a considerable number being from Runcorn. Mr. H. Bratt, of Northwich, presided, and Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., occupied a seat on the platform. On the motion of Mr. James Handley, J.P. seconded by Mr. J. Slater, Mr. E. H. Moss, J.P., of Middlewich, was re- elected president for the year. Mr. E. Milner was appointed treasurer on the proposi- tion of Mr. R. Shaw, seconded by Mr. Hewitt. Mr. A. Fletcher moved that Mr. R. Shaw be chairman of the Executive Committee. He remarked that this com- mittee did a great deal of the work of the association and it was very important they should have a man at the head who had kai experience of an extensive character in elec- tioneering. He knew of no man so fitted to discharge the duties of chairman as Mr. Shaw. (Applause.) Mr. Newell seconded the motion, which was carried meant- moasly. Mr. Shaw, in acknowledzing his appointment, oh-served that they were in a very peculiar position when thee com- menced the last election, but he 'thought they might all congratulate each other that it was brought to a satisfac- tory issue. (Hear, hear, and applaese.) Farther than that they did all they could to bring it to a peacabie issue. (Hear, heard) If there was steything he liked it was carry- ing on work in as peaceetile a way as people would let them. (" There's a good deal in that" and laughter.) Tlhey weiald do it peaceably if they could; but like the Welshman said to his son -"We will do it.." (Laughter and applause. In eulogistic terms Mr.. J. R. Frith moved the re-appoint- ment of Mr. A. Fletcher as hoe. sec., and the restitution was seconded by Mr. Jelin Thompson. Mr. Brunner desired to Ray how heartily he thanked Mr. rletcherfrror the good workhe did last year, and hew cordi- ally he ventured to assure him on his ,own behalf and on behalf of those present that they had. the utmost respect far him—that they admired him as a man, end loved him as a neighbour. (Aliplause:) The motion was carried. and Mr. Fletcher briefly replied, annorrncing his determination to do all in his .power for the Liberal cause in theluture as he had done in the,rast. (Applause.) The following vice-preeidents were elected:Z— -ee-8ton: Mr. Thomas 'Rigby, of Overton. Barnton : Messrs. Peter Boulton and A. V. Sleicher. Davenham : Mr. W.' H. Moreton, -I,ef twich 'Grange. Halton: Mr. J. lieLello.

Marston: Mr.-Johrson Fletcher, Middlewich : The Revs. F. Minton (vicar) and G. K. Walker (Congregaticnalist) ; and Mr. Joseph Millieseton Northwich The Revs. W. Gelley and F. Carter; Messrs. H. Brett, H. Hurst, R. Capes, and James Thomas. Over and Wharton : Messrs. •Joseph Slater, Charles Johnson, Thorn= Pickering, Thomas Gibson, and Joseph 'Pools. •Weaverhante Messrs. William Davidson amid Joseph Trickett. Runcorn: Messrs. T. Handley, S. Taylor,:J. Simpson, R. N. Davies, G. L. Davies, J.P., SpeehmaneW. Ockleston, and F. J. Norienn. It was decided, on the suggestion of Mr. W. Handley, the agent, that the chairman and -secretary of each polling district should be co-optative members of the council. The Executive Committee was .then formed, the Runcorn representatives being Messre. B. Knivehon, J. R. Frith, S. Pope, Themes Riley, William Jepson, and Michael Costello. Mr. James Lukes represents Halton. Mr. W. Handley submitted the amended rules of the association, and, on the motion Of Mr. Brunner, they were referred to a small committee for'consideration and report. After some discussion it was resolved' that the next meet- ing of the Council shouldte held at Runcorn. Mr. R. Shaw spoke of the nececsity.of obtaining improved polling arrangements for Weston Point. Mr. W. Handley replied that an effort was made last year to get a polling station for Weston, but it could not then be accomplished. Another attempt would be made. If there were say inconveniences at other places he should be glad if the secretaries would 'communicate 'with him. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Brunner said if the agents on both sides would agree there would be very little difficulty in getting the magic., trates to agree. Mr. Handley said that was done with regard to Weston. Mr. B. Kniveton proposed a resolution congratulating the ! Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone on his'return to office, ex- pressing unabated confidence,in him as leader of the party, • and declaring the fullest assurance that he would introduce such a measure as would maintain the integrity of the Em- pire while meeting all the reaeonable demands of the Irish people. He remarked that, above all other questions, the Irish question demanded immediate attention. It was a problem which would tax the +best energies of our best states- men. A penetrating intellect, a sound judgment, and a sym- pathetic heart, and an ev'en.banded justice would be required, and in Mr. Gladstone all these qualities were admirably blended. (Applause.) They hoped and believed that he would be the means of .pacifying Ireland—and that upon just and honourable conditions; and that when the history of the work of this Government came to be written, it would have to be recorded that• England's great commoner, assisted by the rank and file of the Liberal party, brought tranquil- ity, loyalty, and prosperity to that unhappy country. (Hear, hear.) If that be accomplished they in the Northwich Division of Cheshire would have the gratification of know- ing that through their representative, Mr. John Tomlinson Brunner—(applause)—they -did their part to assist their noble leader in his noble work' (Cheers.) The Rev. W. Gelley seconded the motion. He said be hoped Mr. Brunner would go; hack to London and say "1 have been in touch with my .constitaents and I find they have the fullest confidence in Mr. Gladstone." (Applause.) What had he done'to forfeit that confidence? He bad frightened a few Dukes. (Laughter.) But did they ever believe when the Democracy came into power that there would not be a readjustment of parties—that some of the men belonging to the -Whig Houses would he able to fol- low the people? If so, they had been greatly deceived. He was glad to say that "the Grand Old Man" retained hie position in the hearts of the people. (Applause.) Refer- eeing to the Irish question, Mr. -:Gelley argued that if they scorned the opinion of the-85 Irish members, representative institutions would be destroyed. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) There was neentterauce of Mail.ladstone, nor of any of the leaders of the Liberal party that would give any fsundation for the disintegration of the Empire. The unity of the Empire was safe. The Home Rulers had not demanded that there should be separation. They demanded that they should have control over local matters. And it was quite right too. (Applause.) Mr. R. Shaw supported the resolution. The result of the last election showed, he said, that Conservatism was dying , out, and they must net be alarmed at the large number of the aristocracy being afraid to deal with those questions which many Liberals thought aught to haw been dealt with years ago. It was quite clear that they tad arrived at a point when some means would have to be taken whereby the straggling masses of this country must beetter provi- ded with the means of comfort than they had been in the past. (Applause.) They had succeeded exceedingly well for a considerable time, •becaase of the amount of labour employed by people who invested their capitalln various branches of industry in this country. They had been supplying the world with machinery and; other goods of various kinds; but they could not go on doing that for ever. The 7 must expect .competition from France and Germany. What was then tote done'? In England, when they considered how they were hampered in trade, in pro- viding themcelves and their workmen with that which was necessary, • they found they were taxed in every possible shape for the benefit of the landowners of the country. It was time they should remove. _gently it they could, come of the burdens they had been ,bearing for so long a ,period. 'This -could only be done by preventing seme of those erien taking from the National resources more than it was possible to Epend, when thousands of unemployed men in the country were desirous of working and earning their support, if only the means of doing se were provided. He believed they were getting nearer to the point when a rereedy would •he found,and he had great confidence.in,the man now at the head of affairs being able to accomplish the work in a way that would be acceptable to all except those who were too nerrow minded to part with that which they never ought to have had. (Applauea.) The Rev. W. 'Vause moved a resoletion expeessing satis- faction at the result of the recent election in the. Division in returning a Liberal member by such a large majority, a result which had vindicated the passing of the Franchise and Redistribution Acts as a just recognition of the Liberal principles held in that part of Cheshire. Mr. 'Vause de- scribed in humorous terms the discomfiture of the Tories, and observed that they might congratulate themselves that they had sent not only a Liberal candidate but a Liberal member. There were plenty of Liberal candidates who were net Liberal members. (Hear, hear aqui applause.) They believed that Mr. Brunner would support measuses of a really Radical type. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner read some verses, entitled h‘ The triumph of Liberalism." which were well received. Mr. G. E. King seconded the motion, which was curled by loud acclamation. Mr. Brunner, MY, on rising to respond, was received with ; loud cheering and the waving of hats. He remarked that be had never had greater pleasure than he had had in doing I 1 the work they wanted him toed° in London. He knew weil I,they wanted him to assist in getting rid of the Tory Govern- ment, and he had done so. (Applause) They might de- pend upon it that he wonld go back from nothing he had said as a candidate so long as he was a member. fie had been very much encouraged by what he had seen in the first week be spent in the House of Commons strength and ; dignity in the leaders of the Liberal side, contrasted with the utmost feebleness and impudence, in the leaders of the Conservatives, The Bradlaugh question had been before i them for years; but when the question came before them ; last the leerier of the Tory party put himself into the posi- tion of being sat upon by the Speaker. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that during the year the association would do some ; valuable educational work. As their member, be aska for ! their support in an attempt he intended making to upset the Weaver treat. As one who wished well to the salt trade, he wished the management of the trust to be in the hands of ; the tollpayers. He also wished to see the question of com- pensation for subsidence settled by the property owners and MU proprietors in absolute harmony. (Hear, hear.) A.d.

div.head: NEW GOVERNMENT.
div.p: THE NEW GOVERNMENT.

1113L.V.ING OF THE CABI:TET.—The first meeting of Mr. Gladstone's Cabinet was held on Monday at the Prime Minister's official residence ire Downing-street, all the mem- bers'being present. Mr. John Morley had an interview of nearly an hour's duration with Mr. Gladstone prior to the general meeting of Ministries. The deliberations of the new Cabinet lasted for three and a quarter hours. It is under- steed that the principal topic of discussion was the attitude to 4)3 taken by the Government with reference to the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. The question of Fcgislation for Ireland alto occupied a considerable portion el the sitting, and a committee of the Cabinet was appointed for inquiring into and reporting on the manner in which it ~.ean best be approached. Another Cabinet Council was held at noon, on Tuesday, at the official residence of the First Lord of the Treasury, Downing-street. All the mem- bers were present when the Council otmmenced except Lord Her schell. Lord Aberdeen called at the Premier's house while the Cabinet was sitting, and remained some time. Lord Herschell attended the Council at two o'clock. A London correspondent writes :—I have very good reason for believing that Mr. Gladstone will submit his proposals with regard to the government of Ireland in the form of re- solutions, on which he will invite the judgment of Parlia- ment.

The Queen has been pleased to approve of the following appointments I—Solicitor-General. Mr. Horace Davey, Q.C.; Judge Advocate-General, Mr. J. Mellor, Q.C. On Wednesday Mr. Gladstone and a number of his col- leagues had an andience of the Queen at Windsor, in order to go through the usual formalities in connection with their appointments in the new Ministry. TEE GRIMSBY ELECTION,—LNOTHER LIBEELL VICTORY. —The polling at Grimsby for the seat vacated by Mr. lieneage's acceptance of the office of Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster took place on Friday, and the votes were counted next morning. The result was declared as follows

Right Hon. E. HENE AGE (L) 3,390 Col. ;CAMPBELL WALKER (C) 2,330 Majority 1;060 At the General Election the figures were—Heneage, 3,714; Walker, 2€97; majority, 814. NEWCASTLE ELECTION: RETURN OF Mn. The coanting took place immediately after the close of the poll, and the result was as follows : John Morley (L) ...._... 11,170 C. F. Hammond (C) 8,449

div.head: PRIMITIVE METIEDISM. CONFERENCE AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: PRIMITIVE METIEDISM. CONFERENCE AT EARLESTOWN.

The third and closing conference in connection with the Warrington, St. Helens, and Earlestown circuits of the Primitive Methodist Connexion to consider the hest means of still further promoting the work of God was opened in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legie-street, Earlestown, on Monday afternoon. The preceding gatherings had been held at 'Warrington and St. Helens, and were marked with con- siderable earnestness. In this respect, however, the closing gathering exceeded its predecessors, and in addition, the congregations who assembled in the afternoon and evening were' larger and more representative of the three districts as- sociated in the movement. The Rev. F. NeShimmin, resi- dent minister, conducted the proceedings, and among the gentlemen present were the Rey.4.:Pickwell (St. Helens), Rev. J. Calvert (Warrington), and Messrs. W. Cox and Jas. Lawless (St. Helens), T. Rollasen and Owen (Widnes), Tit- , chett and Taylor (Warrington), T. Clarke, J. Woods, E. ' Dickens, F. Bagnall, J. Taylor., Lane, Peers, Goodwin, ac. (Earlestown). After singing and prayer, an appropriateportion of scrip- ture was read by the Rev. F. N. Shimmin, who subsequentlV expreesed the pleasure he felt at seeing web a goodly num- ber present from the twocircuits which bad previously extended their hospitality, and which they in the Earles- town circuit were now holding ferth to there. The previous conferences, he added, had proved a great spiritual blessing , and be had been pleased to observe in their own church that these who had attended them had displayed inure cour- age he their professions of faith, and expressed a more in- tense ardour to save themselves and others. He -concluded by expressing a hope 'that t hey would feel perfectly free to offer any suggestions and use every liberty they possessed to good advantage.—Mr.Dring, the local town's missionary, said he had wholly given himself to the service of God and the interests of humanity, and the great desire of his life was to discover the true element of power, and to so bring it to bear upon others that they might be won to the Saviour.—The Rev. J. Calvert (Warrington) bore testimony to the inspiration hehad received and the impetus which had been given to his own church by the suggestions made and the renewed life imparted by the previous meetings.--The Rev. J. Pick- well (St. Helens) spoke in the same strain, after which Mr. 'Owen urgeda necessity for modifying the method adopted at-class meetings, and specially urged the necessity of a closer study.of God's word with the vieweto a higher de- velopment of Christian life.—.llrs. Lawless (St. Helens) thought much good mieht be done by small bands of fe- males undertaking a personal oversight of •tenior scholars belonging to their eabbath schools.—Brief addresses were also delivered by Messrs. T. Clarke, W.eCox, Rollason, eic.ethe proceedings being interspened with earnest prayers andhearty singing of hymns. The aompenv afterwards adjourned to the infaets' vestry connected with the new school in Lord-street, and here a comfortable and enjoyable tea was provided. Over fifty persons sat down. The ladies presiding over the tables were Mrs. Shimmin, Mrs. Holyock, Mrs. Hall, Mrs. Lone, Mrs. Lane, Mrs. Price, Mrs. Peers, Mrs. Pendry, and Mrs. Ban- ton. The, conference was resumed in the chapel in the evening, when there was an increased attendance. The Rev. F. N. Shimmin again presided. The Chairmen explained that those conferences had been arranged in accordance with a elecision of the district committee which transacted the besiness for the Liverpool district, so asito give minis• ters and laymen an opportunity of speaking about subjects likely to awaken thought and to produce a higher tone of spiritual.life. He oiJserved that the conferences at War- rington and Bt. Helens had deepened the spiritual life of the people, and he hoped they at Earlestown would nct be be- hind in giving evidence that God had blessed .them. He urged them•to seek a fuller knowledge of spiritual life and get away from tke sentimental sickly milk and water re- ligion which they were in danger of falling into, and to grasp the truth, becoming a people distinguished at once for piety, good sense, and a knowledge of God's word and a deeper interest it their fellow men. They had been blest in the past history of the church, and he never knew a church to get en -where there was division and no unity. He strongly appealed to them to line as true men according to their professions at home and outside, and in extending the hand of fellowship to his- friends he hoped that they would be united and true one to another, and then the Lord would bless theme--Mr. W. Cox (cf St. iielens), pointed out that there was still a great work Cor the church of Christ to ac- complish, and impressed upon them the necessity of mov- ing forward with .the times. If the world was to be saved they must be more earnest and devoted in their labours, and he hoped they would all realise the great reeponsibilitv that rested upon them.—The Rev. J. Calvert (Warrington) urged that notwithstanding the great work that had been done by the different sections of the church of Christ there was still a great work to be done. But they were encour- aged by one passage of scripture that it was not by strength nor by power, but by the spirit that much could he accom- ,plished.—Mr. Owen (Widnes) and others also spake.

FALL ,OF LIYERPOGL EXHPITION BUILDINGS. FOUR- 'MEN Mrra INJIMED.—A serious and alarming accident took place on Tuesday afternoon at the ground being built upon for the purposes of the Liverpool Exhibition, to be opened on the let May nezt. The exhibition buildings are rapidly progressing towards completion, a large portion of the material •used for the Antwerp International Exhibition being utilised in the election of the various sections. On Tuesday afternoon, as the erection of the south-west annexe was being proceeded with, a large number of men were en- gaged on the iron framework. Without warning of any kind, rbeentire framework collapsed, the whole falling in, as a spectator describes it. "just like a pack of cards." The building was erected in a series of rooms. One of the latter was noticed to quiver and give way, and in a few moments the whole of the structure crashed to the wooden flooring below, with a noise like a peal of sharp thunder. The most alarming rumours were circulated, the first being that 100 men had been killed or injured. As a matter of fact, about 30 men were at work on the building, 14 of whom sustained injuries, two of them Seriously. All were taken to the Royal Infirmary, where it was found that six were so slight- ly injured that they could be treated at home without danger. No delay in opening the Exhibition is anticipated from the accident. On Wednesday one of the injured men died at the hospital. -84-Eui2Tsas—whose professional labours necessitate long In- tervais between meals—nothing will be found so exlallarat,ng, e"lfortlug, and capable of sualabaing exhausted natum as CadbareirOccos, ravanteed absolutely pure.—Advi.

SOCIETY. On Tnesday evening the annual meeting of the Warring- ton Auxiliary of this society W4S held in the Co-operative Hall, Warrington. In the absence of the Mayor through indisposition the chair was taken by Mr. J. R. Buckton. There were also on the platfarm the Rev. C. F. Moss, of Southport (late London Missionary Society in Madagascar), the Rev. J. E. Symons (district secretary), the Rev. J. Yonge, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev. J. Warnock, Rev.W. H. Williams; Messrs. R. Garnett, E. J. Guest J.P. (secretary), and W. Owen (treasurer). Mr. B. J. GUEST read the annual report, which stated that no such figures as would be used to enumerate the issues of the past year were ever employed before ; no such funds as were there recorded were ever received before ; no such field as was there desc-ibed was ever cultivate(' before. In the first year of the ninth decade of the society's exist- ence, the committee bowed themselves down before God in humble thankfulness for an open door that no man had been able to shut; for a balance sheet in which liabilities of £231,000 had been met, and payments made, with a bal- ance still remaining towards the engagements of a fresh year ; and lastly, and chiefly, for a circulation, the wide world over, of four millions of copies in whole or in part of the Holy Bible of God. This circulation exceeded by a million that of last year, and was more than a quarter of a million beyond the highest figures ever reached before. It was the year of the Denny Testament, the "little book" of which in less than nine months 955,000 copies had been taken out of the society's hands. That number nearly ap- proached the society's entire circulation in all languages in the year in which their late noble president, then Lord Ashley, took the chair of the society for the first time. It was the year in which the claims of women have been more fully recognised, and the Word of God had been carried in the hands of women in every Eastern land where organised work was possible. Above £2,000 this year had been spent in that way. It had been a year of large opportunity large- ly unforeseen. English soldiers had read the Acts of the Apostles where once an Ethiopian dwelt of great authority, under Cardace, Queen of the Ethiopians, and under their pro- tection entrance had been found for two efforts to preach Jesus—in his own Gospel—in regions almost inaccessible. It had been a year of financial surprises and deliverances. The society had felt, as was to be expected, the depression of the times. The free contributions from auxiliaries, the main stream of its revenues, fell from £62,000 to £58,000; but what the living could not spare for the society's treasury dropped into it from the hands of the dying; the legacies, which for twelve years past averaged £24,000, rose last year to the sum of £53,000. It had been a year of sorrows of unusual poignancy, of anxiety and cares; of moving acci- dents too, and sudden deaths; but the work had never once been straitened for lack of means. God had buried the workmen, but carried on the work. The free income of the society for the Year ending March 30th, 1885, had amounted to £144,970 4-s 3d, while the sum received for scriptures sold, both at home and abroad, had been £108,693 198 Bd, making, with £lOl 14s 5d received on account of the Rox- burgh Fund for colporteurage in Bengal, a total of £253,765 18s 4d. The expenditure had been £231,006 9s 7d. Their committee felt that they should not allow that opportunity to pass without recording the loss the society had sustained by the death of some very prominent supporters. Amongst these were the late the Most Hen. the Marquis of Cholmon- deley. the Right Hon. the Earl Cairns, and the late :John Hampden Fordham, who were all vice-presidents. But the society mourned with deepest lament the decease of a vener- able and beloved president. At Folkestone, on let October, 1885, the Right Hon. the Earl of Shaftesbury, K.G., de- parted this life in his 35th year. He had been described as the first amongst his contemporaries. His greatness con- sisted in his goodness. His position, his talents, and his worldly substances were consecrated for the good of humanity; and wheresoever a Bible meeting was held, there also should his good deeds be spoken of as a memorial of him." (Applause.) Mr. Wee. OWEN (treasurer) made a statement with refer- ence to the finances of the local branch, from which we give the following particalars:—Dr. e February 17th. Balance, £so 17s 4s; public meeting, Warrington collection, Ll 15s 2d ; Moore collection, £2 is 4d; collected by Miss Dutton, .0 Is; Padgate meeting. collection, £3 16s 6d; collected by Mrs. Garnett, £l3 8s 9d ; collected by Mr. John Guest, ,C4l is; bank interest, 19s 6d ; Mr. G. Powl- son, for sale of Bibles, £24 18s ld ; total, £156 18s 86. Cr.: March 2/st. Payments for Bibles, £l7 Is ; "Examiner" Office' for advertisements. 4s; Mackie and Co., for placards, dm., £2 6s; Mr. Powlson, for reports, £4 6s ; other payments for Bibles, £54 78 86; free gift to Parent Society, £5O; balance in hand, £2B 7s 10d. Mr. Owen added that their Bible stock at the depot at the close of the year preceding this amounted to £29 16s lid; to-day it amounted to £67 Is. They had got a large stock in hand, so that anyone could be supplied without delay. (Applause.) The Rev. E. C. E. CARLETON, in moving the adoption of the reportseexpressed their regret and his own that the Mayor was not able to be present, as he had never previously failed them when he had been solicited to preside over those meetings. (Bear, hear.) The reports which had been read were records of a successful year, and he was sure they were very much indebted to Mr. Guest for his allusion to the great loss the society had sustained in the death of Lord Shatter bury. On this occasion when they were hold- ing their annual festival in honour of the Word of God, it was a matter of congratulation to them all that they ' had not to do much in the way of vindicating the Scriptures, as he thought there hardly ever was a time whem there was so little in the way of assault made upon God's word by the free thinker and unbeliever. In times past they seemed to have gone , through a sert of religious crisis, attacks had been made on the Christian faith and the word of God had been assailed in a way which was perhaps a little bit disquieting to many Christians. They had had their men ef science and their historical critics, but it was a source of satisfaction that their attacks had passed away, at least far the present, and had prod aced no permanent impression upon men's minds calculated to do any injury to the Christian religion. He remembered some time ago seeing a letter written by Pro- fessor Tyndall to the Times, and he was pleased to ind that Professor Tyndall claimed as a source of pride to himself that he was descended from the great William Tyndall who was we of the translators of the scriptures about the time of the „Reformation. That was a matter of great satisfac- tion to Christian people, because Professor Tyndall was one , of those men who used to cause them a little anxiety, the freedom of his criticism and the want of ceremony he usually displayed in dealing with the convictions of Chris- tian people being such that they hardly knew what might be the results which he would ultimately bring about. But it seemed to him (Mr. Carleton) that it was returning sobriety of judgment on the part of Professor Tyndall, as he was advancing into snaturer life, and it was very re- assuring. They, of course, knee, these assaults upon the Christian faith arose up periodically, and he had no doubt they should have them rising up again. The perms who assailed and thought they were going to overthrow Chris- tianity always reminded him of those sanguine individuals who sometimes fancy that they were going to discover per- petual motion, but who always fouled there was something wanting essential to the completion of the work. (Ap- plause.) Mr. R. GARIZETT seconded the motion for the adoption of the report. The Rev. C. F. Moss, in supporting the proposal referred to the work being done abroad, and especially in Madagas- car, with the aid of the Bible Society. The Church of England Missionary Society, he said, supplied the bible in 70 different languages the Wesleyan Society in 30 different languages, and the London Missionary Society in 15 lan- guages, besides he did not know in how many dialects. By the aid of the British and Foreign Bible Society each of these missionary szeieties as enabled to give to the various heathen nations the bible in their own tongue. (Ap- plause.) The reports were then adopted. Mr. E. J. GUEST read the following list of officers for the ensuing year :—President, Lord Winmarleigh ; vice-presi- dents, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., and Messrs. Peter Itylands. M.P., J. G. McMinnies, W. Beamont, S. Rigby, George Crosfield, John Crosfield ; treasurer, Mr. William Owen ; secretaries. tbe Revs. E. C. E. Carleton and John Yonge, and Mr. E. J. Guest ; comnsittee, Messrs. G. Powl- son, J. Smith, W. Barlow, M. Bowden, R. Cook, J. Guest, R. Garnett, Ziba Armitage, Lewis Reynolds, R. A. Naylor, S. Chandley, J. Fairclough, W. D. Jeans, and J. R. Bucliton, with the Rev. J. E. Symons (district secre- tary).

The Rev. J. E. SYMONS moved the adoption of the list. Referring to the death of Lord Shaftesbury, he said he did not think there could be a more appropriate epitaph for that nobleman than the one framed for President Garfield, viz.:—

Life's fight well won, Life's work well done, Life's race well run, k..ow comes rest. Lord Shaftesbury was a remarkable man, and more so than perhaps any of them had realised. He might give them the opinion of two men wide as the poles asunder in their theo- logical ideas, and neither belonging to Lord Shaftesbury's ',denomination. Mr. Spurgeon said "he did not know who the second was, but the first man of the age had passed away when Lord Shaftesbury died." (Hear, hear.) One day Cirdinal Manning came to their bible house for a copy of the Persian bible, and as he was being shown round the house he stopped in front of the portrait of Lod Shaftes- b. ury and said "every man, woman, and child in England, imepective of their religious tenets, ought to hold the memory of that man in reverence as long as they live." (Appliwle.) Cardinal Manning added that whilst he was a commissioner for the housing of the poor they bad Lord Shaftesbury two days under examilAtion, and never until then did he know what England owed to Lord Shaftesbury. (A pplanse.) The Rev. J. YOICGE having seconded the proposal, the list of officers was adopted. The meeting was then brought to a close.

Mr. Childers has replied by letter, dated the 15th inst., that this offer of assistance will be considered.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

It is authoritatively stated that Sir Charles Lillie has no intention at resigning his seat for Chelsea. A lady named Mary Ann Smith, widow, 49 years of age, shot herself in a Manchester hotel where she had been stay- ing since Wednesday last. EXECUTIoN.—George Saunders, fisherman, was hanged at Ipswich on Tuesday morning for the murder of his wife at Lowestoft, on Christmas Eve. Mr. A.. G. Peel, the second son of the Speaker, has been awarded the Peel Medal at Harrow, thus earning the same distinction as his elder brother obtained last year. The Marquis of Bute has promised to give £l,OOO towards the erection of a hospital at Merthyr, provided £2,000 is subscribed by other landlorth, mineral agents, tfr.c. On Monday, at a special general meeting of the Brltisk and Foreign Bible Society, the Earl of Harrowby was chosen to succeed the late Earl of Shaftesbury as president of the in- stitution. KAY'S COMPOUND, a demuloeat anodyne expectorant, for Coughs a:AI Colds. • bold by all Chemists, 9kd, Is, Is lid, 2s 9d.—Adat.
Lord Ranclolph Churchill has resigned his position on the committee of the St. Stephen's Club, in consequence of a gentleman who was nominated by his lordship having been blackballed.

At Crewe railway works, on Tuesday, the support of a large crane gave way, and the crane itself fell down bodily. Several men were felled to the ground, three of them being frightfully injured. A mysterious package has been left'at Swansea Hospital, which, on being opened, was found to contain 50 sovereigns. Upwards of £I,OOO has been received in the same mysterious manner during the past two years. In the Court of Session (Edinburgh), on Tuesday, the St. Andrew's election petition was decided in favour of Sir Robert Anstruther. Mr. Stephen Williamson, of Liverpool, consequently loses his seat in Parliament. The Rev. George Lamb, who two years ago was the president of the Primitive Methodist Conference, died on Saturday morning at his residence in Hull somewhat sud- denly. The deceased, a native of Hull, was 77 years of age. He had been in the Primitive Methodist ministry for a period of 55 years_ __

FIRE AT SEA.—The steamer Caledonia, of Glasgow, was burnt at sea on Saturday afternoon, about 60 miles south- west of the Start. She was laden with paraffin, which caught fire and destroyed her. The master, Captain lofts, and crew-20 in number—escaped in the ship's boats, ana were taken on board the steamer Richard Kelsall, which landed them at Portland on Sunday morning.
Public Analysts have submitted CAnnumr's Cocci to close tests, and the result has atways proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Beware of Imitations.— Advt.

A WINDFALL.—A coal dealer named Day, resident in Leek, has received information from the Court of Chancery that his claim to a sum of £15,000 is fully admitted. The money originally belonged to an uncle, who was an officer in the East India Company, and has more than donbled it- self during the long time it has lain in court. A brother, who is a country postmaster, and a sister, a poor widow, share the windfall.

MORE MAGISTRATES.—On Tuesday morning the town clerk of Macclesfield received a communication adding to the borough commission the names of Messrs. J. W. H. Thorp, Peter Johnson Eaton, J. Somerville, M. A. Cohen, W. T. Birchenough, and W. B. Brocklehurst. The appoint- ments were made by the late Lord Chancellor, who formally asked the opinion of the Town Council, which declined to give any. - Fire are Conservatives and one Liberal. DEATH or PRINCIPAL TULLOCEL—The death is announced of the Rev. Dr. Tulloch, principal of St. Mary's College, St. Andrews. Dr. Tulloc-h was one of the foremost men in the Church of Scotland, and for upwards of 40 years he has been lahorously preaching, lecturing, debating, and writing books, essays, in magazines, and newspaper articles mere or less bearing directly or indirectly on Scotch theology and ecclesiastical controversies. He died at Torquay on Satur- day, at the age of 63 years. ATTEMPTED MURDER AND SUICIDE.—On Tuesday after- noon, at 40, Clarence-street, Dublin, James Byrne, who had been station-master on the Midland Great Western Railway, but was discharged on account of ill-health, attacked his sister with a poker, striking her on the head and inflicting injuries endangering her life. He then attempted suicide by cutting his throat with a razor, making a frightful gash. He and his sister were taken to the hospital in a pre- carious condition. During the past week Byrne looked de- jected.

TERRIBLE BOILER EXPLOSION.—SERIOUS DESTRUCTIOS. --On Tuesday morning, at Exhall Colliery, near Coventry, a large boiler exploded with terrific force, shattering work- shops and everything else with which it came in contact, and severely injured the fireman and another workman. The boiler, which was comparatively new, was blown comple- tely out of its bed, a large portion of it being found in a field 700 yards away. Hundreds of panes of glass in the engine shed were shattered, and a portion of the manager's house wrecked, Che roof being lifted from a room in which a child was sleeping, and who escaped unhurt. Four large coal waggons were blown over and wrecked. The damage is estimated at £3.000.

ALLEGED MURDER OF A. WOMAN AT BIRKENHEAD.—At Birkenhead Police Court, on Saturday, Robert Travis, land- lord of the Swan Hotel, Great Sutton, and Eliza Platt, living at Great Sutton, were charged with the wilful murder of Mrs. Jane Mclntyre, sister of the female prisoner, aged 33 years, Mersey-road, Rock Ferry. A man named Dickinson went to the police station about ten minutes past two on Saturday morning and said something bad happened at the deceased woman's house. The police went into the house. and on going. into the back bedroom they found her in her night-dress lying on the floor, in front of the fireplace, dead. Her night-dress was saturated with blood, and her head and face were also covered with blood. A pair of tongs, broker into several pieces, covered with blood and with particles of hair sticking to them, were found in the room. The prisoner Platt was found in the room, and her dress was all over blood, and the male prisoner, who had jumped through the window, was found in the yard in an unconscious condition. The prisoners were remanded to await the verlict ef the coroner's jury. " NIGREY."— " ERNEST LI ig WOO D." A I LORD RANDOLPH CHURCHILL ON IRELAND —Lor.., D Churchil addressed his constituents in South Paddington on 1 Saturday night, at the Gymnasium in Bayswater. The noble lor.l, referring to the defeat of the Conservative Go- vernment, said it fell because of a hostile majority com- posed entirely of the party led by Mr. Parnell. and it fell because the Conservative Government had announced their intention by the aid of Parliament to suppress the National League in Ireland. Why Lord Salisbury's Government succumbed in that manner was because the Irish party had very good reason to know that if Mr. Gladstone were in power, so far from suppresoing the National League, it was his firm intention to make over the Government of Ireland to the hands of the League. Lord Randolph proceeded to explain why the late Government had not renewed the Crimes Act. What Mr. Gladstone proposed was a repeal of the Union, and that was really a policy of imminent civil war. Mr. Parnell would find the task of conquering the Protestants of Ireland a very hard and dangerous task. THE REPORTED MURDER OF A MISSIONARY BISEIOP.—The Church Missionary Society, having telegraphed to Zanzibar for further particulars regarding the reported murder of Bishop Hannington, has received the following reply : Zanzibar, Friday, eight p.m., Usogna, Oct. 31.—Two eye- witnesses hete ; Bishop proceeding with 50 men ; Lapri- Boned eighth day. Buganda messengers return. All led to execution. Four escaped. Jones waited Kairrondo. Waits caravan two months." The Church Missionary Society I take their telegram as indicating that the two men now in Zanzibar actually witnessed the murder of Bishop Hanning- ton. The Bishop was within three or four days' march of Uganda when the King sent to kill him, and he was im- prisoned with his 50 men while messengers were sent to the King for instructions. When these messengers returned the whole party were led out to execution ; but four of them escaped, and of these four two are now at Zanzibar, and it is thought that they actually saw the murder com- mitted. The society, however, hopes almost against hope I that the Bishop may still survive, and they will not defi- nitely accept the fact of his death until confirmed beyond every possibility of doubt.

DEATH OF LORD CARDWELL—The announcement or ti • death of Viscount Cardwell, which took place at To-quay on Monday, will be recsived with regret by the Liberal party, of which he was a distineuished member. The founder of the family was Richard Cardwell, of Blackburn, who married for his second wife Miss Elizabeth Stott, of Manchester. Their only son, Richard, had three sons. The second son, John Cardwell, settled as a merchant in Liver- pool, and, having married Miss Elizabeth Birlev, of Black- burn, became the father of the future peer. 'Mr. Edward Cardwell was born 24th July, 1813. either in Salford or in Liverpool. He first entered the House of Commons in 1842 as member for Clitheroe, and became one of the band of young men of marked ability who formed the personal fol- lowing of Sir Robert Peel, and who joined with him in those commercial reforms which Peel extorted from the Tory party, but only at the price of their undying hatred. In 1847 Cardwell was elected for Liverpool. and then for the city of Oxford. He sat for Oxford until he finally left the House of Commons for the House of Lords. He had a long official career, filling various offices of. State. In ,1868, when Mr. Gladstone succeeded to the leadership of the Liberal party, Mr. Cardwell undertook the onerous duties of Secretary for War, and in that position carried through Par- liament a reorganisation of the British Army. The series of measures necessary for this purpose were naturally the snb- ject of warm discussion and opposition, some of it based upon political motives, and some of it emanating from pro- fessional critics. In needed great force of character, tact, and patience to complete this transfoimation of the instru- ment of national defence. On leaving office in 1874, Mr. Cardwell was raised to the peerage. The title be selected showed his respect for the name of the family and the county with which they were identified. He entered the House of Lords as Viscount Cardwell of Ellerbeck, in the county of Lancaster. His county seat was at Ellerbeck Hall, near Chorley. His marriage was childless, and the title therefore becomes extinct with its first possessor. prinaEsTrox.—The main cause of nervousness is indigestion, and that is caused by weakness of the stomach.
