BRIDGE WATER NAVIGATION. The annual meeting of the proprietors of the Bridgewater Navigation Company was held on Friday in the Memorial Hall, Albert-square, Manchester. Mr. J. W. Cropper, caair- man of the company, presided. , The CHLIRIIhai moved the adoption of the report, an aloe street of which we have published and explained the charges, under the head of capital account. He would say a few words about the revenue account, because that was of is. terest to the people of Manchester at the present time. Under the head of maintenance it would bef found that the full amount had been expended, as compared with previous years, reaching 8 per cent. of the receipts. This expendi- ture had been incurred, not only because it was right to keep the property in good repair for the shareholders, but bec- se it would be unfair to allow the canal to fall into anyt ag like disrepair if it should be taken over by the S ip Canal Company. The directors intended to maintaia this efficiency as long as the canal remained in their hands. (Hear, hear.) The total pet cut- tage of expenditure this year, as compared uith previous years, was rathgr in farour of the company. It amounted to 70-8 of the receipts for maintenance, traffic and general charges. This seemed an enormous per cent- age compared with railways and other carrying companies, nut it was less than last year, when it reached 81,1 per cent. This led him to remark that some people seemed to think that the amount charged for the sale of the concern . to the Ship Canal Company was exoessive. He wished to remove that impression, for it was not correct. During the time the canal had been in the hands of the Navization Company they had spent upon the one item of maintenance between £300,000 and £400,000. (Hear, hear.) The Ship Canal Company had paid into a joint account to the credit of the Bridgewater Navigation Company the sum of £20,000. That sum wculd he forfeited if the arrangement were not carried cut. In the interests of the different classes of shareholders the directors thought it was only fair that as the accurnmalations which now stood to the credit of depreciation of steamers and the risks upon the river Mersey had all been taken from the annual profits of the concern, they really were the pro- perty of the open stockholders and, therefore the directors felt it was their duty to give the open stock-holders a proportion of those accumulations, because if the Ship Canal were net carried through, and the deposit money were forfeited, it would be perfectly within their rights and power to replace these accumulations to the different funds from which they had been taken to the extent of £20,000, or 4s bonus per share. If the Ship Canal were carried through, his private opinion was that as these accumulations had been taken from the profits, it would be the duty of the directors to give to the open stock-holders a farther bones, so that there might not be so large a balance to be considered wlten the division of theft:lnds took place. He thought it would be a right and fair thing to do this. Some geetlernen bad asked how tbe directors were going to divide tke sum they expected to receive from the Ship Canal Company. He had no further answer to give to that question beyond what was stated in the circular issued last September. Mr. N. BUCKLEY (deputy chairman) aecondcd the mo- tion. e The motion was adopted unanimously.

ALLEGED NEGLECr.—At the Prescot Petty SeSSiOnS, OD Tuesday, three brothers named Martin Mullen and Michael Mullen, labosrers, Widnes, along with John Mullen, labourer, Hapton, near Burnley, were summoned to show cause why they should net contribute to the support of their father, 78 years of age, an inmate of the Prescot Union Workhouse. As the case required the presence of two mag- istrates and there was only one (Mr. H. Bright) preseut it was adjourned to the next court.

Pgascon Scßoor, Boa.np.—The monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board was held on Monday everting. w•,,tt there were present Messrs. W. L. Evans, J.P. (in the chair). W. Goldsv,rorth, J. B. Sanders, T. P. Hewitt, H. Fogg. The return of attendances,&c.. durine• the month ending 12tr, Ft b. was submitted.—The Board briefly considered the questl_rt of arrears in school fees, and the teachers of the schoDls were ordered to further report upon the subject at the nert meeting.—Miss Harris, head mistress of the girls' schco; reported that she had engaged Miss Mary Match, of Pres- cot, as a candidate on probation for pupil teacbership in the girls' school.—The clerk was directed to write to the over- seers that the Board would be glad if, when the " call" is made, it might be promptly paid to the Board's account, as their account at the bank would be overdrawn,

REFRACTORY PAFPERS.—Before Mr. H. Bright at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, William Robinson, William Brown, and William Bright, were placed in the dock on a charge of refusing to perform work allotted to them at Whiston Workhouse. Mr. William Williams, por- ter at the workhouse, stated that the prisoners were admit- ted to the vagrant ward on Sunday night. On Monday morning they were each given 41ba of oakum to pick. That (Tuesday) morning it was found that Brown and Robinson had picked only lithe while Bright hal picked I.lb. The amount given to them was what they might reasonably have nickel—The prisoner Bright said the witness had told him that he ought to be tied to a horse's tail and kicked to death, and Robinson expressed his willingness to stop at the workhouse until he had finished it.—The Bench.: If you go into the workhouse you must do the work allotted to you, and you will have to go to prison for 14 days.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS

The fortnightly meeting of the Present Board of Guar- dians was held at thks Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday forenoon. Mr J Leatherbarrovr presided, and there were also present the Revs T Chambers and J Barnacle ; Messrs W Newsome, W Birehall, J Jacksoe, W G- Ashton, J Fisher, J Griffiths, T Sadler, J Kenwright, J Ellision, J T Hall, T Eatock. J Matthews, R Leigh, H Hultx e, T F Hill, R TUSOD. W Tyrer, W Swift, T Heald, P Longton, and S U Hartley (clerk). XVORKHOUSE STATISTIOS.—The workhouse master reported there were 508 persons in the workhouse this week, against 516 last week and 444 in the corresponding pericd of last year. The vagrants relieved numbered 64, against 39 in the corresponding week last year.

EXPENDITUEE.—The clerk submitted an estimate of pro- bable expenditure during the half year ending 29th Sep- tember. It amounted to £20,300, to which he had added 10 per cent for contingencies, making a total of £22,334. That was exactly the same as in the cntresponclieg period last year. In reply to Mr. Longton, the Clerk said he e 4 not think it was poesible to curtail the estimate in any way, and it was unanimously adopted. TUE DISTIIMSS IN PSESCOT.—The Clerk read a letter'" from the Local Government Board asking if there was any exceptional distress in the Preeco: Union, and if so, they would be glad to receive any saggestions from the Guardians as to dealing with it. He also read a reply which he had prepared. It stated that there had not recently been any material increase in the number of applications fur rell,f, ad the Guardians believed they would be able to deal with any distress that might arise. The Guardians, however. had information that in Prescot township there were 400' or 500 watchmakers out of work in consequence of tee de- pression in trade, and the Board were at a loss to know haw to assist them because they had not applied for relief. He asked if the Government had any work in connectich with that trade which could be given to the Preecot men. Mr. Newsome observed that he knew fram personal experience that many of the watehmakeets- were in deep distress, and they bad too moot- respect for themselves to apply for relief. He therefore moved that the fetter be sent to the Local Government Board.—The motion was carried—rho Clerk remarked that he had received a letter from the Pall Mall Gazette on the same subject, and the Guardians decided to allow it to lie on the table.

THE MEDICAL OFFICED FOB RAD7rorw.—The Clerk ex- plained that since the last meeting a medical gentleman had taken up his residence in Rainford, having purchased from Mrs. Millner, the practice of her late husband Dr. Millner.— The Rev. J. Barnacle moved that Dr. Andrew Murdoch, of Rainford be appointed district medical officer and pubic vaccinator for that district in place of the late Dr. Millner. —The motion was passed.

THE WOOLTON ASSISTANT OVERSEER.—The appointment of an assistant overseer for the township of Woolton was next considered. The Board agreed by ten votes to nine to reduce the remuneration from (id in the pound collected to 5d in the pound, after which the four candidates for the post, selected from the applicants, which the Citric stated, in reply, to a ques- tion, numbered about 200, were called into the room. They were Elijah Baxter, 12, Churcn-road, Wootton; Thomas Pennington, 2, Queen's-terrace, Tarbock-road, Huyton ; John Sadler, Widnes ; and John Spencer, Halewood. Messrs. Pennington and Sadler declined to accept the situa- tion at the reduced remuneration, and the Guardians voted for the appointment of either Mr. Spencer or Mr. Baxter. The voting was by ballot, and each candidate received 11 votes. The chairman thereupon gave lai3 casting vote in favour of Mr. Baxter.—The meeting then concluded.

LORD SALISBURY ON THE IDISII QUESTlON.—Speal.ing on Wednesday night at a banquet to the four Conservat ye mem- bers for Hertfordshire at the Hotel Metropele, Lord SAlis- bury, replying to the toast of his health in cenuection with the House of Lords, congratulated the Conservative party on the victory gained in the metropolitan counties, which he believed was largely due to the teersonal influence of the upper and middle classes, and which influence would be- come more and more extended as time progressed: He Justified the resignation of the late Government, although the vote really had no direct reference to Ireland, because the moment the Government proposed to demand obedience to the law a combination of Liberals and Home Rulers %vas arrayed against them. He did not complain of that act, except that he failed to sea what the Prime Minister was going to do in the case of Ireland, especially as he had issued a letter of inquiry, which, if it brought him at the lowest estimate a proper number of replies, would occupy him over three years in perusing. Mr. Gladstone had no policy with regard to Ireland. He was fiseing for one, as he did in regard to the Soudan and European affairs, but an alliance formed with the Parnellitee would certainly be fatal. He expressed his dread of the dexterity of Mr. Glad- stone as an old parliamentary band in dealing with the Irish question, and cautioned the country against the securi- ties that would be proposed, because a Parliament in Dublin meant the supremacy of the Legislature in Ireland, and that meant the making of an independent nation. Doubtless England might recover her ieipremacy at the cost of civil war, but the greatest cost she would be put to would be in. I regard to her honour, which had been too much trifled with lalready in Afghanistan, Africa. and Egypt.

this "Socialism made plain" during the last few months, and to do Mr. HYNDMAN and his friends justice they did not spout nonsense of this particular kind at the demonstration in Trafalgar Square. Their object, it may bet, was to incite an unruly Mob to immediate violence and, if so, they rimy be said to have secured a certain tneasure of success. So far, they have shown rnore aptitude for destruction than for con- struction; they may raise a row now and again, but with such principles as they ad- vocate they will not renovate society. Let US by all means that are just and reasonable develop such State Socialism as will tend to remove all impediments to the progress of the people—society gaining strength through the strength of the individual to conquer in the struggle for existence ; but, to do this on a basis which shall be sound and permanent, , We must have something better than the Socialism of the Democratic Federation.

. THE political education of the agricultural Class is making favourable progress. As was shown at the meeting last week of the Warrington Farmers' Club, tenants are be- ginning to tire of being toyed with by their landlords. The hard times are making re- forms in the land laws a matters of life and death to tillers of the soil; and some of the raore intelligent and receptive of them have , already come to The conclusion that it is a Waste of time to look to the Conservative Party to help them. There is a feeling of disgust at the way in which Conservatives re- turned from agricultural districts voted against , Mr. BARCLAYS amendment to the Address. Mr LEADAM, the Liberal candidate for the Altrincharn Division at the last election, has been taking the bull by the horns at the an- nual meeting of the Farmers' Alliance which was held in London on Monday. He moved, and gave good reason for his motion, "That inasmuch as the efforts of the Farmers' Al- liance have been systematically opposed by ithe Conservative party in and out of Parlia- ruent, the Farmers Alliance resolves hence- , forth to abandon its attitude of neutrality, and to constitute itself an organization for agricultural reform by means of the Liberal Party." The motion was seconded, and several members expressed their approval of it; but urged that a resolution of such im- Portance—affecting the basis of the organisa- ie. lion—should not be passed without due notice being given to all the members of the fact that it would be brought forward. As it was Mr. LEADAIIfS object to get 1 the question ventilated rather than to Obtain a snatch vote,he withdrew the motion, after some discussion, a request being made . to him that he would read a paper, on the at- titude of the two political parties, at a con- ference to be held for that purpose. It may be doubted whether, looking at the matter from all sides, it would be wi§e for the , Parmers' Alliance to ally itself with the liberal party. It would drive some farmers out of the organisation, and prevent others from coming in who might under ordinary Circumstances be Liberalised by contact with Liberal minds. There is no reason, however, "by the question should not be debated, or for that matter, why a counter proposition Should not be discussed for making the Far- liners' Alliance a Tory institution. It will at east clear the air, sand enable the members to see where they stand. It is a good sign atat, at the same meeting, Mr. PARSONS, of . ants,was successful in inducing the members to insert in the " Objects of the Alliance " the following clause :—"To encourage an increase in the number of small holdings, so , as to provide for a natural growth of the rural Population." Hitherto tenant farmers have been somewhat undecided in their attitude With regard to ihe work of Mr. JOSEPH ARCH. . 'hey cannot forget that he was the means of the wages of the labourers being raised, and their• holding aloof for a time from the new : _crusade is not unnatural. But they now see What is coming, and know that they have ' Inore to gain by standing shoulder to shoul- der with the labourer than by going cap in hand to the landlord. The latter has had his day. he has stood in the way long enough, but 0 the order is given him—he must "move ,11.,,
"TOUCH AND• GO." ; l‘lr. Biggar denies the rumour as to his itiitended retirement from Parliamentary life. Q. Biggar is not a retiring man.

Love, love. love—it's ju4 like a dizziness, And won't let a poor body go about his business. This old couplet precisely describes the con- dition of a young fellow named Ball, who has just been bound over to keep the peace for persistently annoying two sisters, living near Frodsham, by trying, amongst other little attentions, to kiss them when leaving chapel. Ball is said to be affected in the head as well as the heart. He should be tied to his mother's apron- string, or otherwise looked after.

Lord Salisbury in his speech on Wednes- day was indiscreet enough to talk about "vacillation and uncertainty of policy." Per- haps tie was thinking of the way in which his colleague in the House of Commonslaboured, on the first night of the session, to prove that there was an absence of serious crime in Ire- land ; and then, in less than a week, was induced to stultify himself by announcing the need of a measure for suppressing the National League. Oh Frailty, thy name is Salisbury! •

General Wolselev, lecturing on General Gordon, in London, on Saturday, told •a singular story of Gordon's generosity and indifference to money. He started from London along with -Colonel Stewart with £4OO which had been furnished them. Stewart, describing their arrival at Cairo, says—" To my horror there was- a horrid old man, stone blind, who came down to see him, and Gordon—who appeared to have great admiration for him seeing him in dis- tressed circumstances, immediately gave him —X300." Very generous, very heroic ; but it suggests that Gordon was not the man, after all, to be the leader of an expedition.

In our last issue we founded a remark upon the Dilke Divorce case upon what seems to have been an inaccuracy in the report which we received by telegraph. The following im- portant sentence appeared in several journals with the two words which we have placed in brackets, but which words were omitted in our account :—.‘ Mr. Justice Butt, in giving judgment, said that Lto say] respondent had been guilty of adultery with the co-respon- dent, and at the same time to dismiss the case as against the co-respondent was a state of things which t first sight did not look quite reasonable; but when it came to be considered there was nothing unsound." It will be seen that the omission in our report of the two words "to say" makes all the difference between a positive and a hypo. thetical statement on the part of the judge. It gives ir Charles Dilke the benefit of a doubt to which, it would seem, Mr. Justice Butt thought he was fully entitled.

FRESH DAILY.
LOCAL NEWS.

MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN, RUNCORN. Mission services have been conducted by the various ministers in the town during the past week. Seaman and boatmen have attended in moderate numbers. WIDNES ROUNDERS CLUB.—Members of local rounders' clubs will be glad to hare that the committee appointed for the purpose have aaranged dates for the challenge cup com- petition of the National Association during the ensuing summer. Both the Widnes and the Simms' Cross clubs are drawn for the senior cup. RUNCORN WATERWORKS COMPANY.—The half-yearly meeting of shareholders will be held on Monday next. The directors' report to be submitted states there ie a balance of £6BB lie 10d on revenue account, and it is recommended that £525 shall be devoted to the payment of dividend at the rate of 31c1 per cent., and that a balance of £163 us 10d be carried forward. RETIREMENT OF THE COLLECTOR OF CUSTOMS, RUNCORN. —Mr. F. Semen% collector of H.M. customs, Runcorn, is about to retire on superannuation. Entering the service as an outdoor officer at Preston in 1846, Mr. Samons by his force of character and the energy and zeal he displayed in the performance of his official duties, has risen through the successive grades to his present honourable and lucrative position, and he well deserves the ease and comfort he is about to seek in retirement. Hai:role CASTLE—It will be remembered that some time ' ago a portion of the ruins of the castle at Halton fell into the road below, when a young man from Runcorn, who was passing at the time, was seriously injured. The walls were made good by direction of the Secretary of the Duchy of Lancaster, whose property the castle now is. On Mon- day night the same portion again gave way' but happily without any accident. The damage dene will be far in ex- cess of that done on the former occasion. MAGISTRATES WANTED AT WIDNES.—For the conveni- ence of the maeistrates of Widnes the session day has re. centle been altered from Wednesday to Thursday, but the difficulties of the Bench are not yet overcome. Mr. W. H. Kershaw, proprietor of the Drill Hall, was present on Thursday to apply for a theatrical license, but as only three magistrates were on the bench, the application was ad- journed to Woolton. Besides those present all the magis- trates were either away from the town or ill. FUNERAL OF MISS ROUGIER, AT RUNCORN. The re- mains of Miss Marie Rougier, of York, sister-in-law to the Rev. Canon Barclay, whose death was recorded last Satur- day, were interred at the Parish Church, Runcorn, on Satur- day morning. The first mourning coach contained Mrs Barclay, Miss A. Rougier, Mr. George Rougier, mad Mr. John Rougier ; the second was occupied by Mr. and Mrs Brundrit, Mr. Charlee Rougier, and Mrs George Rougier; the third by Mrs Fester, Mr. John Rougier, and Dr. Mac- Doueall ; the fourth (the private carriage of Mr. S. B. Chadwick, J.P.), by Miss F. Barclay and Mr. Guy. Pre- ceding the hearse was a coach in which were the Revs. J. J. Bryant. M.A. (vicar of Lower Whitley),, T. M. Armson, John Madden, and R. Edwards. The ifer. Canon Barclay, Miss Barclay, and Mrs Bryant were present at the service. In the church the service was conducted by the Rev. R. Edwards, and at the grave by the Rev. J. J. Bryant. The choir, under the leadership of Mr. Johnson, rendered appro- priate music. The body was enclosed in three coffins, the outer one being of polished oak with brass furniture, and they were made by Mr. Henry White. Mr. S. Yarwood supplied the hearse and coaches, and Mr. W. II Rogerson was the undertaker. Beautiful wreaths and floral crosres, the offerings of relatives and friends, were placed upon the coffin. RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMETTEE.—Tbe monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on Monday evening. Mr. F. A. Lake presided, and there were present—Messrs. T. Riley, G. Moss, E. Marvrood, W. J. Shore, and J. D. Jones (librarian.)—The Librarian reported that during the last month 1,831 books lied been borrowed or consulted in the reference department, beinz an increase of 263 on the corresponding period of last year. A commu- nication was read from Mr. J. T. Brunner, 'M.P., who en closed a cheque for £5, and promised an annual subscrip- tion of a similar amount to the library funds. Mr. E. Marwood had also presented 20 volumes to the library. Accounts amounting to £3l 12s were passed for payment. —The Chairman observed that owing to the great extent to which the public availed themselves of the advantages of the reading room and library, it would coon become neces- sary to enlarge their premises. One mode provided by the Libraries Act was the borrowing of money to be repaid in 30 years. The Library Committee could borrow £250, the interest of which would be about £lO per annum. With this sum they could make the library and reading room twice their present size by building on the land adjeinlng. There were, however, some disedtantages in pursuing such a course, and he thought it might he better to get the Com- missioners to enlarge the building and the committee could pay them an increased rent to cover the outlay.—After a 'rig discussion the subject was left pver for further con- Eideratiots. A YOUNG VAGIRS.NT.—WaIter Kinsey, a bey, was yester- day remanded at Runcorn Police Court on a charge of sleeping on a canal boat, and having no visible means of eubsistence. THR WIDNES WOUNDING Casa —Michael Carr, a ynuth, was again brought up at Widnes Petty Sessions, On 'Thurs- day, charged with weund,ng John Riley, a labourer, by striking him on the heed with a piece of McCambridge said the injured man wowd not be able to attend court for some time. He was suffering from a frac- tured skull, and exfoliation of the bone was taking place. Tnat was, part of the bone was coining off, and dangerous symptoms might supervene at any time—The prisoner was remanded for a week. WIFE DESERTION AT WIDNES.—At Woolten Petty Ses- sions, yesterday, Michael Walsh, a labourer, was charized with running away from Widnes on the 17th November last, leaving his wife and three children in such A destitute condition that they had to be removed to Whiston Work- house. The prisoner stated he had been to Swansea, Bris- tol, and London in an attempt to get work, but he had been unsuccessful and had returned to Widnes. He was sen- tenced to 14 days bard labour. ASSAULT ON THE POLICE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Michael Dudley, a labourer, pleaded guilty to being druuk sod disorderly in Ann-street, East, en Sunday afternoon, and also with assaulting P.C. Chambers. The prisoner was taken into custody by Chambers on the former charge. On the way to the police station he threw the constable to the ground, struek him in the face several , times, and made his escape. He was afterwards apprehen- ded on a warrant.—He was fined 5s and costs for being drunk. And 108 and costs for the assault; in default three weeks' hard labour. "THREE MONTHS" FOR SLEEPING OUT AT WIDNES.— A rough-looking fellow, named William Dyer, was brought up at Widnes Polioe Court, on Monday, charged with sleep- ing out and having no means of subsistence. The prisoner was found sleeping in a cabin at the Widnes Alkali Chetni- cal Works. He had 5d in his possession. He was described as an idle drunken fellow, who spent most of his tines hang- ing about corners, and Inspector Wood said he had been 21 times before the Bench On 10 of these occasions he was charged with sleeping in chemical works.—The Bench sen- tenced the prisoner to three months' hard labour.—James Rennie was charged with sleeping in Messrs. Golding, Davies, and C9.'S works on Saturday night. He was lying upon the top of a salt cake furnace. He was committed to gaol for seven days. THEFT . OF A CAP.—On Monday, at Widnes Court, James Mulvey (18), Thomas Brett (19), and William Doran (18) were charged with stealing a cap, worth 9d, from the shop of Mr. Jackson, hatter, Victoria-road. On Saturday night the prisoners went into the shop, and Mulvey said he wished to buy a cap. Mr. Healy, the manager, shewed them a quaetity, and they were handling them for about ten minutes. Mr. Healy observed Mulvey put a cap in his
Sam Hague's popular troupe of minstrels will give an en- tertainment in the Public Hall, Ituncorn, .on Thursday

evening. SAD DEATH OF A WARRINGTON UNDERGRADUA.TE. —On Thursday afternoon, Mr. Edward SchOnberg, an exhibitioner of Exeter College, Oxford, and son of the Rev. M. Schonberg, vicar of St. Peter's War- rington, was drowned while boating on the upper river. He was in a small boat with Mr. E. Glover, al-o a member of the college, and it is supposed that owing to a changing of seats it capsized. Mr. Glover was rescued in an exhausted state by a member of Corpus Christi, but his companion quickly sank. The body was recovered and taken to the college. Mr. Schijnberg was educated at the Manchester Grammar School, and also at the War- rington Grammar School. He gained a scholar- ship at the last named school for Oxford in Decem- ber, 1884.

EiARESBIIRY HIGHWAY BOARD. On Thursday afternoon a special meeting of this Board was held in the Sessions House, Daresbury. Mr. Edward Greenall presided, and the following members were present, viz.. Messrs. Joseph Cliff, P. Percival, Win. Bradford, IL Houghton, Chas. T. Whitley, William Long, Thomas Smith Burgess, and the Clerk (Mr. If. Linker.) The meeting was called for the purpose of considering the correspondence which had passed between the clerk and the Bridgewater Navigation Company, with reference to the repairing of roads under Cliff-lane Bridge and Lumb Brook Bridge. From the correspondence it appeared that the corn- pay disputed their liability to repair the roads, they contending it was the duty of the Highway Board. The meeting was of a private character, but it is understood that the Board has determined to make further inquiries as to their position with reapect to the roads. . _

The proceeds are to be devoted to the NVesleyan library extension scheme. FIRE AT RUNCORN.—About one o'clock on Tuesday morning a fire broke out in the shop of Mr. A. Buck. chemist, Bridge-street. An alarm was conveyed to the police station, and the fire bell was rung, but on arrival of Superintendent Wright and other members d the Fire Brigade the flames had been extinguished by the efforts of Mr. Buck and his son, Mr. 'Harry Buck. It Is supposed that the fire originated through the ignition of a quantity of rubbish in the flue. A large number of brushes were con- sumed and the doors of a cupboard were burned through.

In this cupboard were four canisters of gunpowder, and had the discovery of the fire been delayed but a few minutes the consequences from the ignition of the explosive would have been great. The seriousness of the fire may be judged from the fact that the heat forced the stopper out of a bottle of naptha. The amount of damage is not very heavy. FORTHCOMING MASONIC SERVICE AT RUNCORN.—It will be seen from our advertising columns that a masonic service is to be held in the Runcorn Parish Chinch on Wednesday evening next; when the collection will be in aid of the Cheshire Educational Masonic Ins!itut:on. This institution has been of good service locally, and the Run- corn brethren are anxious this year to send a good contri- bution to its funds, in view of an appeal which they are about to make lot an annual grant towards the education and support of the three young orphan children of their late brother, William Houghton, who for some years was tvler, or doorkeeper, to the Ellesmere Lodge. He will be best remembered as the former apparitor at the Parish Church, an office which he held for eleven years, gaining the good will and esteem of all, by his quiet manner and unvarying civility. The children are left totally unprovided for, and we are glad to learn that the Masons intend to do some- thing for them. If help is wanted we feel sure that the congregation of the Parish Church, and all who remember Houghton, will be pleased to co-operate with the Masons in so good and laudable an object. A Sewer WIDNES POLICEMAN.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, Catherine Hines, apparently about 16 years of age, was charged with stealing a pair of boots, the property of James Henry Southwocd, of 7,* Albert-road, Widnes.—The prosecutor deposed that on the 13th inst. he hung the boots on a nail at the shop door. The same even- ing they were taken.—P.C. Holbrook said he was on duty in Waterloo-road on the previous day, when he saw the prisoner wearing the shoes produced. She alleged that her father had bought the shoes when he was drunk. The ! officer told her she would have to go to the police station with him, and at her request he allowed her to walk a few yards in front so that people would not notice. As they were going along the prisoner bolted down an entry, an.l made her escape. The constable afterwards apprehended her. She was then wearing a pair of clogs, but the shoes were found in an empty house in the entry. She now Pleaded guilty.—Superintendent Barker said the girl led a bad life, and she was committed to gaol for a month.—Mr. Gaskell, senr., told Southwood he had a shoo in which to sell his goods, and be ought not to Du t things in the street. By doing so he tempted people to steal. A CHILD SUFFOCATED AT RUNCORN.—On Tuesday after- noon Mr. T. J. Rideway, the coroner, held an inquest at the Runcorn ?ace Court on the body of Lilian Massey, 10 months old, the daughter of Daniel Massey, labourer, of 64, Nelson-street. Mr. Samuel Coventry wA.s foreman of the jury. Esther Massey, mother of the deceased, said the in- fant had never been healthy, and a few months ago Dr. McDougall told her it would never live. Site insured its life for £5, as she thought that would he the safest plan. On Saturday night her husband, herself, and the child slept together at her mother's house. At a quarter past five next morning the child was lying between them, dead.—Dr. McDougall, who bad made a post-mortem examination of the body, said he was of opinion that the cause of death was suffocation.—The Coroner, in directing the jury, siid that in September, 1883, an inquese was held on a child of Massey's, which had died under somewhat similar circum- stances, and in that case the jury eeturned an open verdict. There seemed to be no evidence that this child had been overlain, but he must point out that the simplest thing might cause suffocation, such as a sheet being thrown over the child's face.—The jury, after a brief conversation, re- tUrned a verdict to the effect that the child was accidentally suffocated.—The Coroner sternly cautionet the patents to be more careful with their children in future. FUNERAL OF IVIRS. POTTER, OF RUNCORN.—After a lingering illness. Mrs. Jonathan Potter, of Pennington House, Runcorn, died on Friday last, at the comparatively early age of 49 yews. The family of Potter have had a long and constant connection with the town, and there was a widespread and profound feeling of regret when the announcement of Mrs. Potter's demise was made. The de- ceased lady was the widow of the late Mr. Jonathan Gooddine Potter, merchant, of the firm of Patter and Sons, Runcorn. She was the daughter of the late Mr. John Whit- taker, of Radcliffe, and niece of Mr. W. Whittaker, of Run- corn. The funeral took place at the Cemetery on Monday morning, and the almost universal drawing of blinds and closing of basiness establishments testified to the respect in which the lady was held. Martin ; in the third, Mr Isaac Whittaker, Mr W J Clarke, Mr Peter Smith, and Mr S C Chorlton ; and in the fourth, the Rev A P Watson, Dr MacDougall, Dr Mangan, and Mr John Simpson. The burial service was conducted by the Rev A P Watson. The body was en- closed in three coffins, the outer shell being of polished oak with brass mountings. Beautiful floral offerings were placed on the coffin by relatives and friends. The choice flowers bad been stipolied and arranged by Mrs Stoll, of High. street. SIR R. A. CROSS ON IRELAND. Sir It. A. Cross on Monday opened a new Conservative Club at Darlaston, near Wolverhampton. He accused Mr. Gladstone of an undue desite for power, and said the right hon. gentleman was responsible for Irish grievances since 1808. He had brought us to the brink of a precipice, but whether he would push us over happily did not depend upon himself. Speak- ing a second time, the right hon. gentleman said that the moderate Liberals or Conservatives must before lonF be in power, and that if the former chose to take ofhce and bring forward moderate measures they might rely upon the support of the Conserva- tives as against the extreme Radicals. As to Ire- land, he claimed that the Conservatives had definite- ly declared against separation, but were ready to grant measures to restore freedom and order, and to increase ihe prosperity of the country. lie placed no reliance on Mr. Morley's guarantees of no separa- tion, and said if they enforced guarantees by the aid of soldiers there would be civil war.

The annual meeting of this association was held on Tuesday at the Lunch-room of Messrs. Ga.-kell, Dea- con and Co.'s Works. Mr. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., president, occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Messrs. H. Gaskell, junr., J.P., Cook, Parnell, and H. W. Deacon (hon. sec).
The Hon. Sec. read the following report of the Execu- tive Committee :

"The committee begs to present its annual report. Man- chester Skip Canal Bill : It was found necessary to lodge the petition authorized at the last annual meeting against the Manchester Ship Canal Bill. The committee worked in conlunction with the Local Board, and the bon. sec. went to London with the deputation from that body and gave evidence befere the Committee of the House of Lords. The points in dispute were ultimately reduced to one, viz. : Wlsether, granted that the canal were made and the navi- gation of the river impeded the Ship Canal Co. should be compelled to provide free haulage for all vessels coming to and leaving Widnes. The Lords' Committee decided that the matter should be left for ebitration should the neces- sity arise. L. 4. IV.- W. Railway Bill : The L. & N.-W. Railway Co. withdrew, at the last moment. the clause in the Dill referring to Garston Dock, and consequently, though a petition against the bill had been prepared hy your corn- snittee,it wasnot lodged. Rates Bills: The St Helens Traders joined your committee in preparing its petition against the Rates Bill of the L. & N.-W. Railway Co., and undertook to pay one half of the expenses incurred. Owing, however, to the withdra.val of the bill, the petition was not presented. Petitions had also been prepared by your committee against the rates bills of the Great Northern and Midland Railway Companies. Petitions against the bills in the foam sugges- ted by the Railway and Canal Traders' Association were sent to Sir R. Cross who presented them to the House of Commons, and a memorial OR the same subject was forwar- ded to the Board of Trade. The committee did not find it necessary to make any levy and, as no bills of interest to the traders have hcan introduced.this sessien, there will he no need for a levy this year. By the case of Hall v. L.B. and S.C.R., it was decided that the Railway Company could charge more than their maximum rates allowed by their Acts of Parliament. Feeling the importance of the quecion at issue, your committee guaranteed, on behalf of the asso- ciation, £25 to a fund raised by the Railway Rates Commit- tee for the purpose of appealing and taking such other ac- tion. as may be necessary."
The statement of accounts showed there was a babnce in hand of £l3 lie Bd. On the Opposition account there was a balance of £iBl 19s 10d.

The Chairman moved the adoption of the report, and referring to the Rates Bill of the Railway Companies drew attention to a pamphlet which bad been published by Sir Bernard Samuelson on the rates of foreign railways. In that publication it was pointed out that the rates for coal and iron and heavy traffic were much less in foreign coun- tries than they were in England. Mr. Muspratt was of opinion that the Government were bound to bring in a P^.ll- - Rates Bill this session, and then the traders of Widnes might have to take some action in the matter in order to maintain the position they bad always taken no, and if pos- sible carried out in regard to this question.—Mr. Cook seconded the 'notion, which was carried. The Hon. Sec. observed that it was an int2resting fact that for the first time during its existence the London and north- Western Railway Company had not introduced a bill into Parliament. There was no other business.

Is A " TRAVELLING JEWELLER" A HAWSER 2—Robert Leyland, of Bold-street, Runcorn, was summoned to Run- corn Police Court, en Alonday, to answer a charge of acting as a pedlar without having a certificate.—Police Clerk Wallace deposed that on the 9;h inst. he saw the defend- 'ant enter a shop in Devonshire-place. He opened a case containing watches and other jewellery, and showed some ladies' watches to a person in the shop. The officer asked the defendant for his pedlar's certificate, and be replied that he had none. He added that he understood that he did not reqnire one, and that his employers were in communication with Somerset House on the subject.—By Superintendent Leah : The defendant had been a pedlar three years' and he had had a license. His license expired on the 12th Jan- uary, 1885, and he had since been hawking without license. He knew that the defendant was hawking jewellery regu- larly.—Leyland, who pleaded not guilty, said he had in- structions from Messrs Harris, his employers, not to take out a certificate.—Mr. Handley said that did: not free him if it was the law that be should have a pedlar's license.—The Defendant : I am not a pedlar.—Police Clerk Wallace said on Friday he saw the defendant, wbo stated that he had re- ceived instructions in a letter from his employers to take out a license at once.—Henry Harris, 104, Corporation- street, a member of the firm, said defendant had been in- structed not to take out a pedlar's license. div.head: VAGRANTS DIARY.
div.p: A VAGRANTS DIARY.

It seems there is method in vagrancy as well as in madness, as was shown in a case beard at Runcorn Police Court en Tuesday. George Stanhope and Elizabetr Jones were charged with begging. The woman was seen by P.C. Dale going from public house to public-house, and the pro- ceeds of each &incitation she handed over to the man, who remained outside. When apprehended he was found to have Bid upon him. The lining of his coat was form(d into one capacious pocket, which was filled with many pounds of bread. Superintendent Leah produced to the magistrate a diary found in the possession of the female prisoner, and in which were given particulars of the travels of the couple from town to town. They had been all through Yorkshire and "the North Countree." but their journeys were only noticeable for the success or failure of their cadging. In one place they had "bad a good tidy; got a good supper and dose, and coppers over." it was a "fair day" when they had got coppers but not inuc!l food and had to " buy in.'; The manner in which the diary was written showed that the woman had received an education above the average, but had now hopelessly degenerated into a profes- sional tramp. Their Statereen7s to -Superintendent Leah as to their relations with each other, made when alone, were somewhat amusing. Tne woman said she was married to the man ten years ago at Crew-, and had had two children. He averred that they were m-orird four years ago at Newcastle, and that they had Lad three children.—Mr. Henry Reynolds sent the prisoners to linutsiord gaol for seven days.

be delivered earlier, bet the turkey was to be delivered fo use on New Year's Day. On the morning of the 30th De- cernber, Hy. Billington, the son who took the order, brough" the turkey to Captain Jones's house, but the cook, who took it on a dish, did not consider it was tit for food. She said it smelt badly and sent for her mistress, who, after examining it, was convinced the turkey was bad. Mr. Billidgton tried to make out that the turkey was good, but Mrs Jones re.- fused to have it, and she told Billington that if he left it till Mr. Jones came home he would do so on his responsibility. As soon as Mr. Jones saw the terkey he sent for Mr. More. the sanitary inspector, who was satisfied the bird was net good. The turkey was subsequsntly taken to Dr. Fox med• ical officer, who examined the turkey and found it in an ad- vanced state of putrefaction; apd to Mr. Norris. a magis- trate, who ordered that it should be buried. Mr. Ridgway also mentioned that the defendan t had sued Mr. Jones In the County Court for the price of the turkey, us 6,1, but judgment went against him.—The following witnesses were then called, and gave evidence confirmatory of the above statement, viz. :—Henry Billington, jun., Ellen Waring, cook of Mr. Jones; Ja.nes Mort. sanitary inspector ; and Dr. Fox, medical officer.—Mr. Ridg way having argued the question as to whether the turkey had been exposed for sale, the Bench said that they were of opinion that was a case in which they ought to convict. At the same time, if it was desired that the case should be adjourned in order that de- fenelant might have the point of law argued, they were willing to adjourn it.—The defendant was represented by his sons, who said they wished the case to be disposed of that day —The Bench then imposed a fine of Is and costs, 16s Bd.

said be did not think the justice of the case would be met by dealing with the prisoners at that Court.—Prisoners were then committed to take their trial at the next Liver- pool Assizes, bail being refused.

IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT- _-- HOUSE -- OF LORDS.—THMISDAY. The Lord Chancellor (Lord Herschell) took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock. A Dill introduced by Lord Denman for the purpose of extending the franchise to women was read a first time.

M INIST F.I:IAL TATEI2III3ST.—EarI GRANVILLE stated that - a Scotch Borough Police Bill would be introduced in that House, and that the Lord Chancellor intended to bring in a Lunaey Bill. With regard to Ireland, a measure would be introduced, but the Government had not had time fully to consider it. The other House would consider finance up to the Ist of April, and after that a measure affecting Ire- land would be introduccl.—The Marquis of SALISBURY thought they were entitled to ask for some better satisfaction than to be referred to the Ist of April for an explanation, and said the Government were treating Parliament with singular levity, and powerful Interests with levity also Earl GRANVILLE replied that the Government would make full statements on the whole Irish question in what ap- peared to him to be a very'short time considering the gravity of the subject. Their Lordships adjourned at twenty minutes after seven.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TECURSDAY. The House of Commons re-assembled this afternoon after the interval necessary to allow of the re-election of Minis- ters. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. Several new writs were issued on behalf of new members of the MiniirrT. ENGLAND AND GREECE.—Replying to Mr. J. Cowen,who asked what course the Government intended to take in the event of the Greek fleet attAckieg Turkish ports, Mr. Glad- stone said it was a matter of full satisfaction that the Great Powers of Europe had been acting together, and in the spirit of that concert the Government would undoubtedly con- tinue to act. They would follow without any deviation the course marked out by their predecessors in office with re- spect to the very important question of peace in Eastern Europe, and they saw no reason to separate themselves from a policy which they believed to be directed to the peace of Europe and to the true interests of Greece. THE LONDON RIOTS.—Mr. CHILDERS, in the course of long statement in regard to the riots in London, said the evidence had disclosed a state of circumstances with respect to the administration of the police which would require his serious attention with a view to an immediate remedy. The right hon. gentleman added that there was no truth in the report that the powers of the Chief Commissioner were cir- cumscribed, or that he made application for powers which were refused to him.

FORECAST OF THE GOVERNMENT BUSINESS. The PRIME MINISTER, in the House of Commons, gave notice that on Monday he would ask for leave to refer the question of procedure in the House to a committee larger than usual. With regard to the Address, the Government proposed to accept it in substance exactly as it stood, to- gether with the amendment carried by Mr. Jesse Collings, as well as the remaining portion down to the close, but awing to the lapse of time it would require some gramma- tical changes. That being the case, the Government would not be able to give their assistance to any other amendment that might be moved. As to the Crofter question, notice would be given of the intention of the Government to introduce a bill on the subject at an early date. The time at the disposal of the Government between now and the 22nd of March, when financial bills for the year would have to be produced, might be usefully occupied in dispos- ing of the Supplementary Estimates of the present year and dealing with the great votes for the naval and military services. With respect to Ireland, the Government did not propose to suggest at the present moment a re-enactment of repressive criminal legislation. Their desire would be to introduce measures of a pesitive and substantial char- acter in respect to social order, the land, and any other matter that requires attention in connection with the future government of Ireland and the method of that go- vernment. The matter was one of great complexity and of enormous responsibility. By the 22nd March he hoped to be able to make some further intimation to the House as to the proposals they might have to make for dealing in, he hoped, a somewhat permanent fashion with the great ques- tion.—Sir M. Hicss-thiecu asked for the precise nature of the grammatical amendments to the Address, and for the terms of the reference on the matter of procedure.—Mr. GLADSTONE promised to place the terms of reference on the ' table, and then to make a statement of the intentions of the Government in regard to the proceedings of the Coin• mittee.

THE ADDRESS AGREED TO.—The debate on tits Address in reply to the Queen's Speech was resumed by Mr. PLUN- IET, who argued that the Prime Minister was skilfully avoiding direct reference to the important question upon which the late Government had been practically defeated and which absorbed the attention of the country.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER held that it was unreason- able to demand from the present Government an announce- ment of a character that the late Administration were unable to make after 6 or 7 months of office.—Lord G. HAMIL- TON contended that the Prime Minister was now adopting the very course of inquiry which he had previously con- demned as both "dangerous and tricky."—Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN urged the reasonableness of allowing the Government time to put forward its Irish policy.—Lord H. CHURCHILL joined in the demand fora more definite statement from the Government and demanded to know why Lord Hartington no longer formed tart of the Liberal 'Government—Mr. GLADSTONE said the Government had before them a grave, heavy, an 4 responsible task, and they should address them- selves to it seriously, not following the example of the noble Lord and saying they must have six months to con- sider before they did—what he did not do in the time— come to a conclusion. He desired to meet the reasonable wishes of the House, and he hoped before long to be in a position to state to the House the views of the Govern- ment with regard to remedial legislation for Ire- land. Sir M. Hicaes-Betacm having defended the action of the late Government, the matter dropped.— Mr. MPARLANE moved as an amendment to the Address the suspension of the power of eviction pending legislation for the benefit of the Highland crofters.—ln the discussion which followed, Mr. TREVELYAN objected to the amend- ment on the round that legislation was at once intended.— The, House divided, the Parnellites voting for the amend- ment and the Opposition against it.—For the amendment, 104; against, 234; majerity against, 130. The Address was then agreed to. PARLIAMENTARY FRANCHISE (TENSION TO WOMEN) BILL.—Mr. COURTNEY, in the absence of Mr. Woodall moved the second reading of this bill.—Mr. Puleston and Mr. Everett supported the motion, which was opposed by Mr. Beresford Hope.—After some debate the bill was read a second time without a division, and the House adjourned at 20 minutes to two.

GOOD TEMPLART. —There was a very fair attend._ ance of members at the weekly sessionnf the Hope of Eariestown Lodge of Good Templets on Monday evening', Brother George Clarke, W. Sec., presided in the absence 01 the W.C.T. The Lodge Deputy (Brother John Warburton) read a number of circulars from the Grand Lodge with re- ference to a mission fund and a benefit fund connected wiria the order, after which the digest of business for the next , District Lodge Session was considered, and the lodge re presentatives were instructed thereon. The evening's Pr?' gramme was "Short readings, conundrums, &C,'and in accordance therewith a large number of selections were given by members. The proceedings were greatly en - • joyed SUDDEN DEATH AT NEWTON COICZON. —A gad ft, of sudden death occurred at Newton Common on We'eenee day afternoon, the deceased being Jane Simile, wife of ee Simm, a collier. On the previous evening she had CO plained of a pain in her stomach, and during t! e night her husband administered a " composition " powder. This seemed to ease her and he left home to go to his wort about half-past five on Wednesday morning. She then le: peered to be in good health, and did not seem any worse x' half-past one in the afternoon when she Was seen be, a neighbour named Margaret Woods. An hour later, hoW• ever, the latter was called by a daughter -of the decease". crying out that her mother had fallen. On Mrs entering the house she discovered Mrs Simm lying dead 00 the kitcnen floor. Dr. Fouleton, of Earlestown, was iriune. diately sent for, but his services were of no avail. In about an hour afterware' the clipping machine and clothes brush were missed from the saddle-room, in consequence of which Beresford at ori,n` gave information to the police. P.C. ELBRESTOWN CO.OPERATTYR SOCIETY.—The quarter meeting of the shareholders and members of the Earl;. town Industrial Co-operative Society was held in the operative Hall, Earle-street, on Monday evening, under , presidency of Mr. J. Latham' president. There was a Logi, attendance. The report of the auditors stated that the WTI were kept in excellent order, and they had had access to el , vouchers and deeds. The balance sheet was a true aeenen,lit of the society's position. The committee in their lot quarterly report stated that they could but express th,e regret that it showed a falling off in the receipts for goo":.„. . sold ; but they believed that it was more attributable tovie7 state of trade in the district than to anything else. e,,,e; while they had to record a fall in receipts, it was pleat'' telt to be able to show that the profits realised were such ; would cause those who had their confidence shaken to ra";id. round the old standard, and help them to increase the ceipte, and thereby lessen the working expenses, thus las lug a steady and satisfactory dividend. The balance die posable after defraying all expenses, including interest anl depreciation, amounted to £3BO 23 2d, which they aesit': them to dispose of as follows: —Dividend to members 00 £3,064 lOs at 2s 5d in the X, dividend on 98 non-member' checks, at Is 2d in the X, and a balance of £4 is 11id the contingent fund. The result of the voting ' that Mr. Latham was re-elected by a majority of 51. Mr. T. fe Haselden was re-elected auditor, and Mr. S. Barrett ere' appointed stocktaker. WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE FESAIVAL. The fifth annual festival in connection aveth the Eari.es: town Wesleyan Band of Hope was held in the Bruns%lc:" Wesleyan School, Cross-lane, on Saturday afternoon. number of fligs and banners had been arranged about the room, giving it an attractive appearance. There was a large attendance, and tbe proceedings were of a very enjoyable character. The Rev. J. Kent, resident minister, presided- After the singing of a hymn an prayer, Mr. Willtara Clare (secretary) read the annual report, which stated Velet the committee thanked God for the work that had done and the seed sown during the year, which they trustee" would bring forth abundant fruit, not only in the sobrieti of the children, but in the power and streogt,ti of the church of God, and thus help to stC4' the gap by which so many slipped away frog' the church every year. The report alluded to the meetings held during the year, and continued that the,' were pleased to say their membership remained about the same as last year, 150, and that their financial position v good, having a small balance on the right side at the end 8 i the year. They hoped a good number of their elder scholars would join the senior division of the Band of Hope* and help to carry on the work mere successfully than the had hitherto done, and they called upon all anxious for the salvation of their scholars to join them in that noble work, and help to pull down the stronghold of sin, drunkenness* and vice; and in trying to build up young people in truth. sobriety, and every virtue. The Chairman next addressed the meeting, and strongly urged the necessity and in.3port- ance of properly training children as the future fathers and mothers to habits of temperance, and 50 WI to contend against the evil influences by which they were surrounded- During the evening the Rev. T. Baine, of St. Helens, el_l9° addressed the meeting. The Band of Hope choir, conduct by Mr. Thos. Clare sang "Open the deer for the children, Miss C. Longworth recited "A girl's speech," and Master Thomas Pickett recited Gammy's resale." Miss mar Clare was then deservedly encored for singing "Save the boy," and she responded with "The butterfly." Mr. T. W. Stanfield was enthusiastically applauded fur a violin solo, "Hope told a flattering tale," and in response to appeals for an encore he bowed his acknowledgments. A pleasing dia.* Logue, entitled "How Sam was changed," was given bY Messrs. T. Robinson, Richard Critchley, John Barr, J. Clarke, Thomas Clare, jun., Miss Clare, and Miss Pickett. 'The outcast baby" was recited by Miss M. A. Webster* and a daet entitled "We are sowing" was nicely sung bY Misses Evans and Eckersley. Mr.- J. Haws was warma applauded for several finely-executed selections on thr, "Fairy Belles," Master S. Marsh recited "Poor Tommt,* Miss M. E. Prescott gave "Nettie's ChriSknas," and Mr. l• W. Stanfield was encored for another violin solo. "Before the constituency "—an amusing sketch—was capitallY represented by Messrs. William Pearson, John H. Profit, Webster, 0. Pickett, and William Clare. Mr. Wl.l. Ram Clare nicely sung "Three acres and ? cow," Master William Lilly gave a pleasant rect.- tatien entitled "Little Tommy's new father," and ele choir concluding the programme with the piece, 6. HarraP for sparkling water." Miss E. L. Greenail presided at the pianoforte. Hearty thanks were accorded to the enter' tainers, speakers, &c.

LIBERAL CLUB DISCUSSION. IRISH GRIEVANCES. The subject of "Irish Grievances" again formed the topic of debate at the weekly meeting of the Debating Class at the Eariestown and District Liberal Club, Fair' dough-street, on Thursday. There was a full attendance' and Mr. W. D. Burdis, of Newton, presijed. There were Moo present Messrs. F. A. R. Neill (Bold), M. Birkbead, T. Foulkes, H. Waywell, G. Ratcliffe, J. Rutter, and others. The Chairman remarked that during the last 100 Y,eeaer! Irish grievances might be ranged under three heads. -au' first was the most intolerable that any :country could ea" perience, namely, a religious one, but thanks to the admiral°. tation of the Liberal party that had heeer/ taken away. The next grievance was the question, and the third Home Rule. The land question Nva' one, he said, which all Englishmen, Scotchmen, and Welsh' men suffered from. In order to obtain the best results fr 0,133, the soil it was necessary to have a free interest in the free right of culture and a security that the reward of thell toil should not be taken from them. That could only bea obtained by the people of England, Scotland, and Reline uniting and working for a reform of the land laws. All' ing to Home Rule he urged that Ireland deserved Inch a measure, though he was strongly opposed to separatiOn To obviate the difficulty created by the animositY Orangemen and Paruellites, the Irish Parliament, if one established, should represent both classes, and from tuft benefits which would accrue Englishmen, Welshmen. all Scotchmen would obtain a share.. (Applause.) Mr. Thomas Walsh then resumed the debate in an hated esting address from an Irishman's point of view. He alit!: ded at some length to the various Irish measures, conarnie' ing on the Compensation Bill, Land Act, akc. He gave 10 stances of the heartless evictions and in replying to remo.reel". at previous meetings said there were many persons wisll.7 to know Mr. Parnell's demands, but the time had not Ye arrived for him to make them known. He believed aol good which would come to Ireland would come frehl she Liberal party. (Applause.) It had been said that go% Rule meant separation from England, but Irishmeu did 1:1:Le want that. Irishmen had hitherto had a share of sours, °ls they only now wanted a portion of the sweets.—lr. leeW,e T. Foulkes replied to Mr. Walsh at some length, and Si there was no doubt Ireland had suffered under its ances. It was surprising to him that discontented 'rum:L-0 had been able to keep so quiet under its grievances as had done. Had the same grievances touched the Eng"fte people to the same pitch he believed they would hive Ma" con' a much bigger row about them.—The discussion ivall tinued by others.

div.head: WIDNES AMATEUR DRAMATIC SOCIETY. PERFORMANCE LAST NIGHT.
div.p: WIDNES AMATEUR DRAMATIC SOCIETY. PERFORMANCE LAST NIGHT.

After an existence of only a few months the Widnes Amateur Eiocutionary and Dramatic Society ventured last night to bring itself into the full light of public criticism, and the verdict on the whole was a highly favourable one. Originated by several local young gentlemen with a taste for the drama, the society now numbers nearly a hundred members, and there is the prospect of it becoming one of the pe,manent institutions of the town. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., fills the position of president, and there is a numerous and influential list of vice-presidents. The secretarial duties are ably performed by Mx. E. M. Davies. As we have inti- mated, the first public performance of the members took place last night, whea a large audience assembled in the Volunteer Hall. The reserved seats were especially well filled. The pieces chosen for representation were the late H. J. Byron's popular comedy, "Our boys," and the farce, "Turn him out," written by T. J. Williams. Before the rising of the curtain, Mr. James White, the stage manager, came forward and recited with appropriate gesture and good effect a pro- logue which had been written specially written fer the oc- caeion. The farce was first presented; but it proved as laughter provoking as ever. Mr. Harry Cookson, as Niced-mas Nobbs, an itinerant vendor of toys was all that could be desired for the part; and Mr. Mackintosh Moke (Mr. Arthur G. Davies) was capitally pourtrayed. Mr. .3barles ickson was a good make up as the fop. Mr. Eglantine Reseleaf, and he made the most of a rather weak character. Julia (Mokes wife), and Susan (a maid of all work), were MR. BRUNNER, M.P., AT RUN 2ORN. respectively represented by Misses Annie C. Davies and Annie Aunter. Mr. John Crosfield headed the subscription list with the sum of £loo—(applause)—and their friends Mr. Monks and Mr. Hough went to Liverpool to ask sub- scriptions from several friends, with the result that £32 was received from the following gentlemen, viz. :—Messrs. M. Smith and Ca., £2; Banks and Ratcliffe, £5; J. H. Rayner and Co., £5; W. Crosfield, £5: Verdin and Sons, £5; J. Samueleon and Son, £5; Bingham and Son, £2 2s; W. H. Stead, £3. Coming nearer home, the following have been received :—Monks, Hall, and Co., £11; chapel anni- versary, £10; Messrs. J. G. McMinnies, £5; R. A. Naylor, £2; H. Milling and Co., H. Thornton, John Nue:aerie! and Co , and F. E. Crosfield. £1 each ; a friend, 5s ; Mr. R. W. Parry, 5s ; teachers and cemmittee, £l6 13s 6d. The total amount raised up to that time was £223 Ss 7-111, which left the SUM of £l3 16s 7,led to be yet raised. Towards that deficit several lady friends had given trays, and he hoped that they would soon be out of debt. They were, however, much in want of an organ or harmonium for school pur- poses. The matter was laid before Mr. Crosfield, who, with his usual kindness, said that they should have an organ, and they could that night say—and they were thankful for it—that success and prosperity had attended their efforts.— The CHAIRMAN subsequently addressed the meeting. They would not, he said, expect any lengthy remarks from him, but he could not let that opeertunitv pass without congrat- ulating the committee and the congregation upon their suc- cess. (Hear, hear.) The sum of £240 was a large amount to raise, and it would be a matter of sem@ satisfaction to them to feel that they were within £l5 or £2O of raising it, because he knew from experience how debt paralysed not only the efforts of individuals, but of congregations. Some people said that it was a very good thing to be in debt, and that a chapel would not prosper unless it was in debt. They seemed to have the idea that if there was sOmething to ask for and aim at in order to get out of debt, that therefore people would give much more liberally. He did net believe that himself, which was perhaps the result of his training. He congratulated them on being able to free the place from debt, because he knew it must have been a very heavy weight. He was glad to see the efferts that they made—and the success which justified them—end he was sure that tlee neighbourhood must be a great deal better in consequence of the efforts. One could not help feeling that the old benches that were formerly used in the chapel must have been stiff and uncomfortable, especially if they had a long sermon, and the change would be very good for all. An organ would tend to make their services much more hearty, and he was glad that they were going have one. Altogether. they were doing a very good work in that neighbourhood, arel must go on and prosper. In conclusion, he urged them to look well to the younger members of the congregation who would take the places of those who were now getting old.— The following programme was alas, carried out: Selections, St. Paul's Handhell-ringers (encored) ; song," Arm, arm ye brave," Mr. Rellian ; " The gates of the west," Mies Bax- ter; song, "Love's request," Mr. Ikin ; song, "Angels ever bright and fair," Miv Davis; song, "The Monarch of the woods," Mr. Bellian ; song, " Within a mile ef Edinbro' town," Miss Baxter; song. "Good-bye sweet heart," Mr. Ikin ;" The hanks of Allen Water," Mies Davis. Mr. George Riley officiated as accompanist.—Mr. William- son proposed a vote of thanks to those who had given their services that evening. Mr. D. Hill seconded the proposi- tion, which was carded with acclamation.—A vote of thanks was passed to the chairman on the motion of Mr. Long, seconded by Mr. Hough (secretary).—Appended are the names of those who gave trays and presided at the tables ; —Mesdames Ashley, Lone, Penn, G. Hassell, John Has- Ford, Dawher, Dale, Hill. Willett, Proud (and Miss Proud), Mellor, W. Horton, Hough, Monks, and David. Monks.
DARING ROBBERIES BY BOYS AT RUNCORN.

Yesterday at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. W. Bankes and Captain C. W. Hazleharst. Thomas Abrams, aged 11, and James Smith, aged niue, were charged with stealing a coat and two pairs of gloves, value 10a, the pro- perty of Mr. John Johnson, manager of a Widnes chemical works who resides in Leinster Gardens Runcorn. On Tuesday ' afternoon last Mrs Johnson sent her little boy to Mrs Soulbv's school, Irwell-lane. He was at that time wearing the coat produced and had the gloves in his pocket. As he was returning home he was met by the pri- soners who told him they had seen his mother, and that she had instructed them if they met her son wearing a light coat with a velvet collar, and a velvet cap, they were to take the coat from him and have it repaired at the tailors. After this statement, the prisoners relieved the boy of his coat. Mrs Johnson, immeliately upon bearino of this, went to the pawnshops, and shortly afterwards -Mr. Craddock, pawnbroker, Church-street. saw the prisoners standing near his premises with the coat in their possession. He captured Abrams, but the other made his escape, but was afterwards apprehended.

Abrams and John Molloy (aged nine years) were now charged with stealing a macintosh, and about 40 silver and copper c3lns (foreign), belonging to Mr. Thomas Leach, tailor and drape, Church-street. On the 12th Januaty the shop was made quite secure. Next morning it was dis- covered that one of the windows at the back had been broken, the building entered, and the goods overhauled. The articles mentioned in the charge were missed. Thomas Green, a boy. deposed that after the shop was clostd Abrams suggested that the three boys, who were playing together, should enter the yard. Abrams and Mulloy did so, and also broke into the shop, returning with the macintosh and coins. With one of the coins they purchased a currant cake at a shop at the bottom of Regent-street, and sold the remainder to a man faatned Finegan, who keeps a marine store in Water-street.

Abrams and Molloy were further charged with stealing a pair of boot, the property of Mess.... Tyler and Sons, Bridge-street. The boots were stolen from the shop door on the 6th February. When the boys were apprehended they were sccos2d of this robbery, and they each charged the other with being the thief. Mary Ann Mnlloy, a young woman, was charged with receiving the boots, knowing them to have been stolen. She was, however, dis- charged. Abrams was now charged alone with stealing a silver chain, a cap, and a pair of mittins belonging to Joseph Abel, of Suffolk-street, on the 10 li February.—Mrs. Abel said the prisoner came to her house and told her he had nowhere to go to sleep. She therefore permitted lairn‘ to stay all night, and next morning gave him a good breakfast. The articles were soon afterwards missed.—lhe prisoner pfeaded guilty.—The parents agreed that the boys should be sum- marily dealt with, and Abrams, who has been previously birched for larceny, was sentenced in the first case to 21 days' imprisonment, afterwards to be detained in a reforma- tory five years. In the other cases he was committed, as a matter of form, to seven days' imprisonment, the sentences to run concurrently with the former decision. Smith and Mulloy were each ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod. •

NEW MARMALADE, 31b. jars 9d. and 10d.—Law- less Bros., 5, Market-place, Warrington.—Advt. Compulsory vaccination does not appear to be -vigorously carried out at Leicester. Returns issued on Weencadav- show that out of 7,279 births, within a stated period, 4,850 escaped vaccination entirely. THE CLERGY IN IRELAND AND M. WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE ,COURT.. MONDAr.—Before Mr. John Fairclough, Alderman Pickmere, and Councillor Greening. MISCELLANEOUS.—James Thompson, for begging in Par- ker-street on Saturday night, was sent to prison for seven days.—Thomas O'Brien, charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-street on Saturday night, w.v.s dismissed with a caution.—Michael Calligan, for committing a breach of the peace by being disorderly in Winwick-street, was or- dered to find a surety for his good behaviour. A VtoLENT CASUAL —James Margetson, a young man, was charged with refusing to break stones whilst a casual inmate of the vagrant ward at the Workhouse. Evidence was given to the effect that on eaturday prisoner refused to perform his task, and broke several windows, doing damage to the amount of Ss 10d. For refusing to work he was sent to prison for 14 days, and for committing wilful damage he was ordered to undergo an additional month's imprisonment. Asserim.—Patrick Roche was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Orford-lane on Saturday, and farther with assanfting two soldiers named John Grady and Michael Barka. It appeared from the evidence that prisoner hit the soldiers, one on the ear and the other on the end of the nose. He was sent to prison for a month. TuESDA.Y.—Before Mr. C. Broadbent and Alderman Holmes.

Bitßam OF THE PEACE.—James Gallagher, a young man, was charged with having committed a breach of the peace on the 13th December last. Inspector Spinks stated that en the day named prisoner and a man named Farrel wets fighting like dogs." Farrell had been previously dealt with. Prisoner was bound over for six months, or, in default of sureties seven days imprisonment. A DESERTER.—James Pickett was charged with deserting from the South Lancashire Regiment stationed at Orford Barracks Prisoner was found in plain clothes in the King's Arms Hotel on the previous day by a policeman, and on be- ing questioned stated that he had thrown kis uniform into the river. In court he stated his clothes were thrown into the "cut." Hr was handed over to the military authorities. _ _ _

DomEsTic DiseonEratENT.—John Bridges, a blacksmith out of employ, was charged with having assaulted his wife on Saturday last. From the evidence it appeared that pri- soner had been iddrink on Saturday, and after some words between them he committed the assault complained of. Mrs Bridges complained that her husband had illused her for a considerable time and was in the habit of using dis- paraging language about her, while the prisoner asserted that his home was net comfortable and that his wife would rather listen to the " jangle " of the neighbours than stop in the house. The case was adjourned for a fortnight to give the prisoner an opportunity of amending his ways.

THrßSDAY.—Before Major Litton. A Nocrunset. FlGHT.—Thomas Foy was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street the same morning. He was also charged with assaulting his father, who, however, did not appear to prosecute. P.C. Corbett said that at about one o'c:ock that morning he heard the sound of glass breaking and went up Foy's entry. Pri- soner's father shouted police, and witness saw the son follow him out of the house and strike him severely. The con- stable and prisoner bad a struggle and, assistance having arrived, the latter was taken into custody. A fine of 103 and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, was imposed.
FnlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds, Mr. R. Garnett, and
Dr. Goinall.

A SUSPICIOUS PERSOlC—Matthias Woods (13), forge hand, was charged wi,l2 being a suspicious character, he having 6een found in possession of some cart springs, re- garding which he gave an unsatisfactory etplanation, and having aiso been convicted of felony. lie was sent to prison for one month, with hard labour. A DISORDERLY Cnenerrna.—Bodelia Knockton, a young woman, was charged with being disorderly and breaking eight panes of glass at the house of her father, 20, Havdock- street, on the previous night.—Sergeant Jones saw prisoner smashing the windows, and said she was perfectly sober at the time.—Prisoner had been eighteen times before the court, and was now sent to prison for a montb, with hard labonr.

ALLEGED ASSAULTS.—WiIIiam Humphries was sum- moned by William Cosgrove for assaulting him, on the 13th inst. The two work together, and complainant alleged that defendant kicked him on the eye. This defendant denied, and said that it was his "hand that did it." He said that complainant need bad hnguaze to him. Defendant was ordered to find a surety for his good bsbaviour.—Ann Griffin was summon d for assaulting Sarah Bibby, OA the 13th inst. They came to words while in a vaults, and de- fendant was alleged to have struck complainant. The case was dismissed,

Charaock, for being drunk at Bartonwood, was fined 5s and costs.—John Clayton, charged with being drunk on the highway at Warrington, was or- dered to pay costs.—Tbotnas Smith was charged with carry- ing a gun without a licence at Poulton-with-Foarnbead. He was fined 5s and costs - - -

A CARELESS PCBLICAN.—James Jackson was charged with permitting drunkenness on his licensed premises at Penketh. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the defence.—ln con- nection with the same case, William Deakin was charged with being drunk on the premises, the Crown and Cushion Inn.—The police gave evidence that Deakin was drunk, and in defence Mr. Davies called witnesses to say that he was not drunk. It was contended that Deakin had a habit of laughing immoderately, and that he was thought in con- sequence to be tipsy when he was sober.—The magistratas did not record a cenviction, but ordered defendants to pay c9ga, Sr(O3TING A TAME PlGl3oll.—John Astell (18) Was tharged with shooting a tame pigeon. Mr. P. Davies pro- secuted, and Mr. A. Browne defended. The bird belonged to a young man named Richardson, who said that it was a very valuable one; but a witness for the defence said that it was not a valuable one. He complained that the flying powers of the pigeon were destroved.—The magistrates fined defendant is, and ordered that he shoull pay 103 to- wards the value of the bird and costs.

DOG CASES.—Thomas Ditchfield, farmer, Thelwall, was charged with having kept a dog without a license on the 11th' February and was fined 2s 6d and costs.—A case against Robert Oldfield, farmer, for not keeping a dog under proper control on the 6th February was dismissed. POACEIING —Joseph Spencer, alias George Tomkinson, was charged with trespassing on certain land in pursuit of game on the 11th February.—P.C. Arthern, stationed at High Leigh,. said that about three o'clock on the afternoon of the day in question he saw three men walking at a sharp pace down the road. They soon began to run carrying, a net with a hare in it, but witness overtook them and got hold of the net and hare, but they prevented him from tak- ing them until he had blown his whistle and attracted someone to his assistance. The three men gave wrong names and two of them bad since absconded. The defen- dant was the only one they had been able to serve the sum- mons upon, and he said he would not appear before the court. —A fine of 40s and cr sts was imposed. or, in default of payment, a month's imprisonment. SUPPORT Or PARENTS, &C. —An elderly Mall named John Bate was ordered to pay is per week Cowards the sup- portof his mother, who is Chargeable to the Altrincham Union.—George Lee was ordered to send his child regularly to Lyinm Parochial School. UNLICENSED GOES—Peter Davies was prosecuted by the revenue authorities for having used a gun without a license, on the Ist December, at Hearly. A fine of 20s and costs was imposed.—Geor iestle; , farmer, for using a gun ge without a license on another person's land, was fined 6d, and costs 14s 6d.
