SANKEY WANDERERS v. BANK QUAY STAR.—Played on the ground of the former, and ended in a draw—three minors each.
LATCHFORD V. WARRINGTON ROVERS (2Nl).—Played on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and ended in an easy victory for the visitors by one try and eight minors to nil.
IVAuutticrroN RANGERS v. FARNSVORTR.— Played at Farnworth on Saturday. At the call of time victory rested with the Raugera by one goal, one try, and one minor point to two minors.

ST. HELENS RECREATION V. OLDHAM BOROUGH.—The re- turn match between these teams was played at St. Helens on Saturday last, and resulted in a win for the home team by two goals, two tries, and three minor points, to one minor point. The weather being favourable a large number of spectators were present. TOTTINGTON V. WIDNES.—This match was played at Tottington on Saturday before 1,500 spectators. The game throughout was very evenly contested. Tottington played down hill, and shortly after the commencement Worthing- ton made a grand pass to Walker, who, after evading several men, dropped a splendid goal from near the half- flag. Nothing but minor points were scored after, Tottington winning by one goal and four minor points to two points. WESTON SHANTERS V. ST. HELENS TRUE BLITES.—This return fixture was played at Weston on Saturday, and after a very exciting game the home team were victorious by one goal, ten minor points, to St. Helens two minor points. The try for the Shanters was obtained by J. Farrell, which Brookes converted into a neat goal. All the home team played a splendid game throughout, especially Walford, Far- rell, and Austin, as did Unsworth, Lunt, and Lilley for the visitors. WARRINGTON ROVERS V. KINGSLEY—The return match between the above clubs was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter at S.lton Park, Liverpool. The home team were well represented, whilst the Rovers had only a moderate team, and played one short; nevertheless a very fast and pleasant game resulted, and when time was called the Rovers were returned the victors by one goal and four minor points to four minor points. It was only towards the close of the game that Allen, by a well-judged kick from the field of play, managed to score the winning point for his side. For the home team the full back played a grand game, whilst for the Rovers it would be unfair to make special mention of anyone, as all played to win and not to obtain individual praise. iiVNCORN y; Cc uEs.—Tile fixture between these two clubs was decided at Runcorn, on Saturday. Runcorn had been drawn upon by the county, and the places of W. Wright, W. Hughes, J. Lewis, and H. C. Speakman had to be filled by promising players from the second team. The greater part of the work rested with the forwards, the backs having comparatively little to do. The game ended in a draw, the Runcorn team scoring a touchdown to nil. The forwards were strong, and fully maintained their prestige; and it was certainly from no fault of theirs that a bigger score was not registered to the credit of Runcorn. Teams : —Runcorn : Back, T. Woods; three-quarter backs, E. Lunt, G. Wainwright, and T. Johnson; half-backs, H. Hughes (captain) and G. H. Andrews: forwards, W. H. Broady, F. Joule, J. Gatley, J. Dean, J. Barnes, J. Hoff- land, J. Clarke, W. Faulkner, and W. Dunbavand. Eccles: Back, Ashton ; three-quarter backs, Worthington, Potter„ and Gorton ; halfbacks, Willis and Halsall ; forwards Fletcher, Munn, Holt, Shrewsbury, Brookshaw, Lythgee, Underwood, Holmes, and Ha m.
yman. ASSOCIATION RULES. Winsiort V. WARRINGTON.—Ptayed on Saturday on the ground of the former, the home team winning hy one goal to nil.

STcrotToX HEATH, ST. THOMAS'S V. SANKEY BRYINERS (Ist TEAMS.)— The above teams met at Earlestown an Saturday, and an evenly-contested game resulted in a draw, each side scorieg 2 goals. PRESCOT V. ST. SAVIOUR'S (LlviraPooL).—These teams met oa Saturday at Stanley Park, Liverpool, the visitors winning by one goal to nil. The second teams were en- gaged at Prescot, the home team winning by twelve goals to nil.

EARLESTOWN WANDERERS V. HAYDOCIC.—This match was played on the ground of the latter on Saturday after- noon in the presence of a considerable number of specta- tors. The game was fast and exciting, but, contrary to general expectation, the Earlestown Wanderers won by three goals to none. NEWTON ST. PETER'S 2ND V. GOIRORNEI ROVERS.—This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday and a pleasant and well-contested game resulted in a victory for the home team by one goal to nil. Smith for the " Saints " played a good game, and Atherton was very safe at full-back for the visitors.

EARLICSTOWN V. Peamma.—The Padiham team who are at Newton-le-Willows undergoing a week's training in view of their match with Burnley to-day (Saturday), encountered the Earlestown team on the ground of the latter on Monday afternoon. Additional interest centered in the game, as on the following Saturday the Liverpool cupho.lders meet Stanley in the fourth round of that competition. Upwards of 700 spectators assembled' and the match proved of a very even and exciting character' The absentees from the Earlestown team were J. Ellison and A. W. Dagnall (captain), whcse places were respectively filled by J. Shaw (Earlestown Wanderers) and J. Jame;. There were also two absentees from the Padihatin ranks, and substitutes were found in W. Hatch (Golborne) and T. Champion (Earlestown Wanderers). During the first half the visitors played downhill and quickly registered their first goal, but the cupholders were not long in equalising the score. This was the state of the game at half time. On the change of ends play was very fast, and both elevens displayed capital form. The Earlestoniar!s had slightly the best of the game, but they could never gam the lead, as the defence of the visitors was brilliant. When time was called each side had scored two goals, and the result was thus a draw. EARLESTOWN V. BLACKBURN PARK-ROAD.—Battliday last was the dav fixed upon for the return match at Blackburn between Ersrlestown and the well-known Park-road Club. Unfortunately, however, the Liverpool cap holders were unable to muster their full strength, and they started from Earlestown with enlv nine men, the absentees being "Jim" Ellison and "Billy "-Rich. When they arrived at Black- burn, however, two substitutes from the Lower Darwen F.C. played for the visitors. The latter won the toss, and during the first half played against a stiff breeze. For a I few momenta the game was very even and fast, but after ten

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1886.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1886.

minutes' play Dagnall (visitors' captain) was seriously in- jured about the knee and bad to be removed from the field. During the rest of the game the Earlestonians played with but ten men. Notwithstanding this drawback they made a decent show against their powerful opponents. whe scored I four goals during the first half. On the change of ends the visitors were thoroughly disorganised. and the clever Park Roadsters, who were in capital form, pressed their opponents. Playing with only ten men, and these including two sub- stitutes, the visitors never became seriously dangerous, but the backs and Appleton (goalkeeper) played splAndidly, the last-named especiady distinguishing himself, and earning the well-deserved cheers of the on-lookers. When time was called Park-road had won by six goals to none. The fol- lowing ten played for Earlestownt—J. Appleton, goal; R. Green and J. Green, backs; J. Duxbury, R. Bowker, and J. Whalley, half backs; J. W. Sims, T. Siddley, J. Livesey (sub.), and R. Whalley (sub.), forwards.

TICE UNEMPLOYED IN WARRINGTON. DEPUTATION TO THE GUARDIANS. On Wednesday a deputation consisting of Alderman Holmes, Alderman Burgess, Alderman Webster, Mr. W. Beamont, Mr. R. Davies, Mr. Armitage, Major Litton, and Mr. Carson, waited upon the Warrington Board of Guar- dians to confer with them upon the subject of an extension of their powers to afford relief to the unemployed people of the town. Before the introduction of the deputation some discussion took place as to the guettiOn of relief. Mr. HARRISON said that a number of gentlemen had con- stituted themselves a deputation to wait ripen the Board for the purpose of _representing to them that there was an ab-

normal state of distress existing in Warrington which re- quired to be specifically dealt with. He believed the ob- ject of their coming there that morning was to ask the Guardians whether, under existing circumstances, which were quite exceptional, they should not relax the strin- gency of the conditions under which relief was at present being granted. We knew that the Guardians had their

nands tied behind their backs in a great meastrre-, and they could not give relief to able-bodied men. He lead no doubt that when that law was shaped there was no lack of work, and the law was made stringent so as to prevent anything like imposition. It was the duty, of the Board of Guardians

, to simply administer the law as they found it, but he be- lieved the Workhouse at the present time was fall to reple- tion. The CAAIRMAX : On the women's side. Mr. HARRISON said the object of the deputation was to see if the Guardians could not ad- minisaer relief under certain circamstances in the shape of test cases, and, all being large ratepayers and persons of position iu the town, to give the Guardians their moral support in any course they might take.—The CLBMC said he had had a communication from the Local
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. ['here were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Appleton, Ratcliffe, Jno. Houghton, W. Houghton, Gibson, Hum- iiihriwe, Jolley, Greening, Blackhurst, Bonnell. Harrison; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk).

feared that many of the people in receipt of school fees as non-paupers really require for their children some help be- yond that of the grant of school fees, owing to the tempor- ary want of employment of the head or other members of their families. This want is perhaps better under- stood by your own School Enquiry Officer and by the School Attendance Officer in the service of the Warrington Corporation than it is understood by otl.ers. Probably if some arrangement existed whereby a discreet selection of deserving cases could be , made from the list of recipients of school fees, and some 1 other than pauper relief be afforded to them, your Board will be able satisfactorily to meet all the difficulties of the posilion until the approach of another winter. I have ob- served that in many cnenties Boards of Guardians have successfully applied to Town Councils to provide temporary useful work for the class of their urban population who ' may be reckoned as ordinary recipients of school fees yet ' not of pauper relief, and it will be well if è similar applica- tion is made by you to the Warrington Town Council, whose School Attendance Committee have especial means of dealing with the subj-ct. The labouring classes in other townships are faring but hardly, yet they appear to be suffi- ciently employed and remunerated to preveat their being ap- plicants far relief, and very little difference exists now from ' the normal extent of pauperism. It is very undesirable to invite an addition to pauperism. The experience of all en- gaged in the administration of relief is that at the best of times, if the opportunity is afforded, undeserving persons, men who will not work when work is available, are the first to come to the front and press upon Guardians their de- mands for relief. It will be a mistake to mix up such per. sons with the deserving and industrious people who want some help for unavoidable reasons, and who ought, if pos- sible, to be relieved without being reduced to pauperism." (Applause.)

div.head: APPLICATION.
div.p: eiN APPLICATION.

The House Committee recommended the granting of an application of the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephonic Company for permission to erect five poles for telephonic purposes in the workhouse premises, on condition that they pay an acknowledgement of Is per pole per annum, make good all damage that may be done in the erection or re- moval of the poles, and to remove the poles on a three mouths' notice.—On the motion ef Mr. APPLETON, seconded by Mr. GREENING, the minutes were adopted..

div.head: PADGATH SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE PADGATH SCHOOLS.

The School Committee's minutes stated that the dector had reported that the general health of the children was satisfactory. Mr. F. J. Williams tendered his resignation as industrial trainer in shoemaking, which was accepted. The Superintendent also reported that the boy John War- rington had been brought twice to the schools after having absconded from the workhouse.—The CHAIRMAN moved, and Mr. JOLLEY seconded the adoption of the minutes.— Mr. BLACTUIUBST suggested that an examination of the schools be made periodically, in order to see if any of the children had parents who were in a position to take charge of them themselves —Mr.Dannysninn said the committee was always making inquiries of this sort, and, as a matter of fact, children were often taken away by their parents when their condition had improved.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: SCHOOL FHES COMMITIHS.
div.p: SCHOOL FHES COMMITIHS.

This committee reported that school fees had been granted in 26 new and 87 old cases, total 113.—Mr. Snica- HURST, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said he was sorry to say that the number of applications was increas- in4 and tbis showed the depression of trade in the town.— Mr. RITCLIPSE asked as to the number of fees granted com- pared to the same period last year.—The CLERK said there was about a third more this year.—The minutes were then confirmed. ALLEGED NEGLECT BY THE NEWTON REGISTRAR.

The CLERK stated that he had forwarded in the usual way te the Local Government Board the report of Dr. Watkins in which he complained of the continued hindrance to infantine vaccination caused by the persistent neglect to give notice to parents and custodians of infants at the time of of birth on the part of Mr. Appleton, sub- registrar at Newton. He had also requested Mr. Appleton to be present that morning to give his explanation.—Mr. APPLETON was then called Intel the room. He said he was sorry to have to appear before them to answer such a charge, but he was sure the vaccination of infants had not been hindered through his neglect OD by any want of exertion on his part. He had done all he could to assist the vaccination officer and Dr. Watkins. He had, however, been kept with- out vaccination papers in December because the printer could not get them done soon enough owing to the election. He could not see why Dr. Watkins should make that report about him.—Mr. HARRISON asked if he ordered his papers a reasonable time before they were wanted.—Mr. APPLHTON : I had not many in hand, but I expected to get them in a shorter time than I did.—The CHAIRMAN: But you have been here many a time for the :same thing.—Mr. APPLETON: I have been here once before.—The CLERIC said Mr. Apple- ton had got into a procrastinating way that was most , troublesome. Dr. Watkins was not the only one that might have preferred a complaint against Mr. Appleton. He could not tell why Mr. Appleton had fallen into that state, but he would nottieo anything when it ought to be done.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE did not think the Board could look over that affair without some censure.—Mr. APPLETON: I hope it , will ; I will take care in the future that it does not happen again. But lam not aware of a single case in which a , child has not been vaccinated through my neglect.— Mr. HARRISON said the same neglect seemed to per- vade .the discharge of Mr. Appleton's whole duties.— The CHAIRMAN said they did not wish to deal harshly with Mr. Appleton, but it was for the Board to say if the clerk should write to the Local Government Board about the mat- ter.—Mr. HARRISON moved that the matter stand over for a month to see if Mr. Appleton would pursue a course which would save him from a repetition of complaints of that kind. Mr. Appleton must, however, understand that that slovenly way of doing his duties must not continue.—Mr. JOLLEY Seconded this proposal.—Dr. DARBYSHIRH said he hoped Mr. Appleton would at once attend to what he had promised to do for the last 10 years. In all the business he had done for the Board both in that and other departments, he had continually shown procrastination.—Mr. GREEN.. IWO Suggested that if these complaints be made again Mr. Appleton'e conduct should be no longer tolerated.—Mr. RAT- CLIFFE said they were always complaining about what took place at Newton. They might be gods at Warrington ; they committed RO faults. (Laughter.) They bad com- plained of the school fees at Newton, but now they had a great increase of tees at Warrington while there was a great decrease at Newton. He believed the Newton district com- pared favourably with any district in the Union. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. HARRISON'S motion was then agreed to.

div.head: COUNTY RATE.
div.p: THE COUNTY RATE.

The CLERIC mentioned that in preparing next half-year's estimate of expenditure he would have to provide for a demand from the county of £2,446 lOs 9d, as compared with sloe 23 7d in the correspoading period of last year, He could only say that he thought it high time they had some control of this expenditure. (Hear. hear.) This was all the ordinary business of the Board. A report of the interview with a deputation regarding the distress in Warrington appears in another column.
At a meeting of the governors of the Bank of England on Thursday forenoon, the bank rate of discount was reduced from three to two per cent.

Caution :—Condy's Fluid bears the name of Condy and Mitchell at foot of every label. Beware of wortra- less cdlourable imitations.—Adet.

div.p: _EARLEST OWN.

DEATH OF A POSTMAN.—Willia.ra—impson, 66 years of age, residing in Oxford-street, Earlestown, died some- what suddenly on Tuesday morning. The deceased was formerly a Lricksetter, but for a considerable number of years past had filled the post of postman for the Burton- wood district. He attended to his duties on the Wednes- day morning preceding his death, but he complained of illness and he went home. He was afterwards attended by Dr. Patterson, but the deceased was seized with several strokes and died as stated.

public entertainment was ,1 given in the Good Templars' Hall. Bridge-street, on Satur- day evening under the presidency of Bro. James Barnard, W. treasurer. There was a good attendance. Songs were given by Brothers T. Gorse, A. Allison, J. McDonald, John Taylor, and Sister Mary Whitty ; recitations by Sisters Sarah and Ann Gorse, Brothers George E. Warburton, A. Warburton. and John Warburton; and raadings by Bros. , J. Barnard, C. E Matthews, and John Taylor. Glees were given by Sisters Harrison, Lord, and Lowe; and Sisters F. Lindsay, Harrison, and Bro. R. Walton. THE PADLEAat Foomar, Dux er Nimrox.—During the present week the famous Padiham football team have been staying at the Blue Bell Inn, High-street, Newton, kept by Mr. Henry Hibbert. Their visit is for the purpose of undergoing a week's special "training" in view of their match with the Burnley P.C. to-day (Saturday.) They have engaged the services of the well-known " Tudsey." Walsh, of Earlestown, as trainer. Their peregrinations through Newton and Earlestown have occasioned consider- able excitement. On Monday they played a match on the Mesnes with the Earlestown first team, and a splendidly contested game resulted in a draw of two goals each. FoorrATH OBsTuumoN. At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, Joseph Barber, an elderly man, was summoned for obstructing the footpath by wheeling a coal waggon thereon on the sth inst. The defendant pleaded guilty.—P.C. Lloyd deposed that he saw the defendant wheeling a coal waggon along the footpath in Market- street, Earlestown, for a distance of 300 of 400 yards. There had been a good many complaints from property owners about the practice. The defendant said he was a poor man and dependent upon his two sisters to keep him from the workhouse.—The Bench said they were willing to let the defendant off on the payment of the costs and providing he would be careful not to repeat the offence.

A rrn-VecaNATons FINED.—B of ore Colonel George McCorquodale, Messrs. R. Houghton, T. J. Gillespie, C. Pilkington, A. C. McCorquodale, and W. F. Gooch, James Parrott, of 42, Sankey-street, Earlestown, was summoned for failing to carry Out a magistrates' order to have his child vaccinated. Mr. John Clark, president of the Earlestown branch of the Anti-Vaccination So- ciety appeared for the defendant, and admitted that the child was not vaccinated. He said the defend- ant did not disobey the order from any vindictive motive, but merely with the idea of protecting his child. It was well understood that vaccination did not protect them from smallpox, but in many instances it caused serious diseases. That was the only idea for disobeying the order. If the Bench could not see their way to—The Chairman (inter- rupting) : That will do, I think the Bench quite under- stands that.—Mr. Ciark : I would ask you to impwie the very lowest penalty you can do in this case.—A fine of 256 d and costs was imposed.--James Grimshaw, 177. Legh- street, was summoned for a similar offence, and Mr. Clarke said be had been asked to request the magistrates to deal leniently with him.—The Bench imposed a fine of 2s 6d and costs.—Mr Clarke also appeared on behalf of Wil- liam Whitley Owen, pork butcher. Bridge-street, who bld been similarly summoned in respect of three children.—A fine of 2s 6d and costs was imposed in each case.

Campbell aad other magistrates, a f:Duil, man named Thomas Ball, residing with his parents Wistribolds Trafford, was summoned for assaulting Flor- ts4lce Bower, at lie.nsforcl, on the 2nd Fehruary;—From the ll'idelice given it a9pearel that complainant was the daugh- 'r Of Mr. James Bower, farmer, Hapsford, near Frodshem, t,le defendant lived three miles away at Viiimbolds raff.nd. During the last five years the defendant had been th,, habit of constantly annoying the complainant and 1:t sister particularly, and his conduct ultimately became ,•"suff.rable. Defendant usually followed them about, try- t kiss them. lie wrote letters to them, besides pei.rpetn- ,llY hanging about the premises; and on one occasion he I,,nabered up a haystack to look through their bedroom 1.2,13cinw. On the afternoon of the in question he came into complainant's house, and went the shippon, where witness and her sister Kate were DilLki-hg. After a considerable _amount of annoyance cons- father cline up, and succeeded in locking defend- in the coachhonse whilst a policeman was being sent t. The officer endeavoured to persuade defendant not to "°Y the girls. He replied—" I will not leays.. them nor 4.lrsalie them." div.p: WIT AND HUMOUR.

The only land restorers—Agriculturists. Woman's one notable invention—Perpetual emotion. Second thoughts are always best. Woman was an after- thought of creation. Why is it that a spotted pony never pays toll ?—Because his master pays it for him. "'Tb but a little faded flower," sang Mrs. Jones at luncheon, when Jones complained that the biscuits were otale.

What an optician says who is not a teetotaller.—When a man sees double, it is evidence that his glasses are too strong for him. Young Hopeful, to his sister: I say, Nell, pass me the butter.—Nell, in a tone of sisterly reproof If what,Johnny ? —Johnny, goaded to desperation by the delay: If you can reach it. A prompter at the Comedie Francaise who had prompted Rachel for years one night put his grown-up son in the box. "Where are you going, father ?" he asked. "In front, to see Rachel play; I have never seen her," was the'reply. A Pennsylvania inventor has invented a new rat-trap, in one end of which is a mirror. This may do for the female rats, but When a male rat notices that the bait looks double he will think he has had enough, and go home. " Ah !" moaned a widow recently bereaved, "what a mis- fortune ! I know what kind of a husband I have lost, but how can I tell what kind of husband his successor will be ?" It is possible to tell the age of a cow by the wrinkles on her horns, but nature has provided no outward signs by which the age of an egg can be computed. Break it gently. " No, sir," said a man, "you needn't tell me a woman ever had her dress pocket picked. I don't believe a thief can discover it. I know I've tried for two hours to find the wicket of one of my wife's dresses, and had to give it up." An Irishman who was given to praising his native isle visited a farm in Maine, the proprietor of which had sus- pended several large pumpkins in an apple tree. He was asked what he thought of the apples. "Very good," he said, "for American apples, but nothing at all as big as we give to the children in Ireland." Th 4 editor of an Omaha religious paper remarks—" We recently hired a coloured man to beat a carpet for us. He had what seemed to us a villanous face, and we watched him aenaewhat closely. We were not surprised when he brought in a bill for four dollars. 'But, sir,' said we, this is too much. You surely vould not cheat a preacher!' brudder,' said he, 'you mull remember dat Pse a preacher too.f , The Yankee says, " How de do ?" the Italian, "How do you stand ?" the Frenchman, "How do you carry yourself?" the Dutchman, "How do you fare ?" the Swede, "How can you ?" the Pole, "Art thou gay ?" the Turk, "May Allah prosper thee ?" and the Quaker, ," How is thee ?" Oat in ae=thetic Montana the usual salutation is, "Hello, cully ; how's yer conduct? Come in and give the internal revenue a boost!" A COMPROMISE.—Scene--Near Braidhnrst; a schoolboy with a bulged-out jacket runs down the road from a festive farmhouse, and passes his father. Father: Hallo, Jamie— whanr ye gann ?—Jamie: Gann for a bottle o' whnsky.— Father : What? I thocht ye vvis in the Baan' o' Hope?— Jamie : Ay, but awm gettin' thrippeace for gaun!—Father, who admires genius, stares after him proudly. HAD MAL THERE !—lnterior of railway carriage Brown, who rejoices in a superabundance of fiery red hair, to Jones, who has no hair at all: I say, Jones—surely you can't have been there when the hair was given out !—Jones: Oh, yes, I was but they offered me only a lot of red stuff; and I didn't take It.—Brown buries himself in his newspaper. The German papers Publish the following " hit " on the Socialists. Social Democrat to soldier: "I say you are one of the people. You wouldn't fire on your countrymen, would you?" Soldier : "No; catch me shooting at anybody !" Social Democrat: "That's the way I like to hear a soldier talk. Sit down and have some beer." The soldier does so. " Now take a smoke." says the Social Democrat, when the repast is over. Once more the soldier complies. "Are there many seldiers in your regiment who would refuse to fire on the people?" asks the Socialist. Soldier : "About twenty. You see I am a member of the band, and we members of the band have nothing to shoot with." COULDN'T STOP THAT Boy.—ROMeyD, a Montclair, N.J., boy, aged five, converses with his friend of equally mature years, as follows: Romeyn : " My pa is going to get me a goat." Fairchild : " I've got twenty goats." R. : " Where are they ?" F. : "Oh, they're down in New York, in pa's office." R. : Why don't they bring them down here ?" F.: "They're sick." A pause. Finally Romeyn speaks: "I saw Anthony's Nose last summer." Fairchild: " I saw Anthony himself." R. : " Anthony's Nose is a rock, and it broke off and fell into the water." F. : " I saw it fall." Romeyn's mother, an interested listener, at this point deemed it expedient to interpose with a moral lesson. "Why, Fairchild," said she," did you never hear of Ananias and Sapphire?" F. : "I knew them both." R.'s mother : "You know, Fairchild, they were struck dead for telling lies." F. : " Yes; I saw them struck." R.'s mother: " Fairchild, do you know where they went? (Very impressively)—They went to hell." F.: " I know it. I saw:them go." Fo'n GIRLS AND WIVES.—A good many husbands are spoiled by mismanagement. Some women go about it as if their husbands were bladders, and blow them up. Others keep them constantly in hot water; others let them freeze. Some keep them in a stew. Others toast them. Some keep them in a pickle all their live& It cannot be supposed that any husband wiil be tender and good managed in this way; but they are really delicious when properly treated. In selecting your husband you should not be guided by the silvery appearance, as in buying mackerel, nor by the golden tint, as if you wanted salmon. Select him yourself. Do not go to market for him, as the best are always brought to your door. It is far better to have none unless von will patiently learn how to cook him. A preserving-kettle of the finest porcelaia is the best; but, if you have nothing but an earthenware pan, it will do. See that the linen in which you wrap him is nicely washed and mended, with the se- quired number of buttons and strings nicely sewed on. Tie him in the kettle -with a strong silk comfortable cord; the duty-string is likely to give way (husbands are apt to fly , out of the kettle and be burned and crusty on the edges, since, like crabs and lobsters, you have to cook them alive). Make a clear, steauy fire, and practise neatness and cheer- fulness. Set him as near this as seems to agree with him. If he sputters and fizzes, do not be anxious; some husbands do this till they are quite done. Add a little sugar in the form of what confectioners call kisses, but no vinegar or pepper on any account. A little spice improves them ; but it must be used with judgment. Do not stick any sharp in- strument into him to see if he is becoming tender. Stir him gently ; watch the while, lest he lie too flat and close to the kettle' and so become useless. You cannot fail to know when he is done. If thus treated, you will find him very digestible, agreeing nicely with you and the children, and he will keep as long as you want, unless you become care- less and set him in toe cold a place.

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

Whilst protecting three bailiffs who were making a seizure at the residence of the parish priest of Tallow, county Waterford, a body of police was attacked by a crowd, and much disorder ensued. CAPTURE OF A MOOXLIGHTER.—On Saturday morning, in Skeenarinky, the police arrested Patrick Quinn, at the house of a farmer named Casey, for being one of a party of moonlighters who attacked the houses of several farmers in the neighbourhood of Charleville on Nov. 20th. The police were admitted to Casey's house after considerable delay, and Quinn was feund concealed in a chest, which the owner re- luctantly unlocked. PETlTlONS.—Resoluticus in favour of granting to Ireland the right to legislate for local affairs were adopted by the Dublin Corporation on Monday, and forwarded to Mr. Glad- stone, Mr. Parnell, and Lord Salisbury. The Corporaticn declare that the granting of a native Parliament would bring peace, contentment., and prosperity to Ireland, and would neither involve danger to the Empire nor to the Pro- testatat minority in Ireland. SINGULAR OUTRAGE.—A singular outrage has been perpe- trated at Limerick. Mr. Ambrose Hall, J.P., was one of the most active promoters of the work of erecting a statue to the memory of Sarsfield, the defender of Limerick on the occa- sion of the siege of King William's army and the capitula- tion of the city. Mr. Hairs name was inscribed on the pedestal of the statue, but within the past night or to it has been obliteratedpapparently with a hammer. EXTRAORDINARY ROYCOTTING.—An extraerdinary case of boycotting occupied the attention of the meeting of the Cork Landlords' Defence Union on Saturday. It was re- ported that Mr. Thomas Sanders, J.P., Charleville, was un- able to procure any provisions in his native town, as he was boycotted by the traders owing., to his having evicted a number of tenants for non•ptyreent of their full rent. Arrangements wereoinade to forward Mr. Sanders necessary aupplies. nu, Int SH SPLIT.—PROBABLE RETIREMENT OF Mn. BiGGAR.—The DuPin Express says :—Mr. Biggar contem- plates retiring from Parliament. The news will cause a great shock in all circles. It is not known for certain what action Mr. Healy ssill take, but he will in all proba- bility retain his seat, but keep out of the kay. It is rumoured that there will be several resignations Of members, who absolutely refuse on any terms to recognise Captain O'Shea as a colleague. AN ALARMING Ptortroo.—A correspondent signing him- self " Celt," writes from Dublin as follows :—" The sweetest and most cherished anticipation to those who have of their own accord joined the National League is t hat they can wreak their vengeance on Protestants. (I say of their own accord becatase it is too wsll known here, and it is a pity that Englishmen do not know it too, that piobablv not oite; fifth of the subscribers to its funds have joined it volun- really.) Children, as soon as they Can speak, are taught to curse the ' Sassenach.' Papist butchers gloat in anticipation over the time when they will have other throats to slit be- eirles those of calves and bullocks, and they openly talk of wading knee deep in Protestant blood." MOONLIGHT RAIDS.—A series of moonlight raids took place the other night at Kilcurnmln, near Killarney. Only three men took part in the attacks, and seventeen houses in all were visited. The men were all disguised ; one of them was armed with a rifle, while the other two only carried sticks. Their mission seemed to be one of plunder. At seven o'clock at night the raiding commenced, and the time the last house, was visited was four o'clock the following morning. IVlartid Doody's house was visited at ten o'clock, ' and £lO were taken away. About two hours subsequently the house of a farmer named Teelan was attacked by the i trio, who, however, were compelled to retreat in 11,,t baste. , In the remaining houses attacked sums varying from 2s. to 1 10s. were demanded and given - DEMONSTRATION AGAINST " LANDLORDISM " IN WATER- FORD—In response to the summonses contained in an es- teestyely posted placard there was a great gathering of far-

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER

LONDON, THURSDAY. Members of the Rouse of Commons flocked down to-day in great numbers for what is practically the opening of the session. It must be said in justice ' to the Conservatives that having committed the original sin of not immediately resigning on their defeat at the elections, they did their best to miti- gate the evil consequences of that action. It would have been much more convenient for the new Government, and greatly to the advantage of the public service, had Lord Salisbury resigned the first week in December, giving his successors opportu- nity for preparing their programme for the new session. But Lord Salisbury, not, I believe, in his own interest, but in that of his colleagues, hung on to office to the very last moment, and having been Premier for something like a fortnight; and after only two Cabinet Councils, Mr. Gladstone finds him- self face to face with the serious work of the ses- sion. But consequent upon the exceptionally early meeting of Parliament leaving some interval for the mischievous and time-wasting process of the re- election of Ministers, the House finds itself sum- moned for the despatch of business only some ten days or a fortnight later than the customary

time. But the evil remains that Ministers having charge of one of the gravest questions ever submitted to Government are called to deal with it with what is practically no measure of time for consultation.. It was too readily assumed that the two Cabinet Councils held on Monday and Tuesday were.occu- pied chiefly, if not exclusively, by consideration of the Irish question. But there is at the beginning of a session much to be done before the chief measure of the session is approached. In ordinary times the estimates are quietly prepared in Decem- ber, and generally engross the consideration of one Cabinet Council, sometimes two. These had to be discussed on Monday and Tuesday, in addition to which there were the peculiar circumstances of the Address to be dealt with, and foreign affairs, which wait for no man, had to be discussed. Ignoring these things, and misled by state- ments of what had passed in the Cabinet Council, the public had come to expect to be put in possession to-day of full details of Mr. Gladstone's new Irish policy. The expectation was dispelled by the announcement in the papers of Wednesday, and it must be said that the situation has been accepted with pretty general admission of the reasonableness of the plea for Ministers. Of course here and there, as was shown in the House this evening, there are unscrupulous partisans who insinuate evil things because Mr. Gladstone, having within the last four days met his colleagues twice, is not prepared with a bill designed happily to re- volutionise things in Ireland. But on the whole the impossibility of such procedure is frankly ad- mitted. In the East of Europe the war cloud seems to be lifting. The Roumeliots have practically obtained the object for which they pluckily fought, and Prince Alexander is confirmed in the fruit of his victories. The painful part of the business is the attitude of Greece. The position of this country is one that naturally excites sympathy throughout England. In 1877, whilst Russia and Turkey had their hands at each others throats at Plevna, Greece might have made a splendid bargain. Either Turkey or Russia would have given anything she asked for assistance. But in deference to the English Government Greece I remained quiescent under the distinct pledge of I being provided for when a Conference should re- settle affairs in the East. At the Conference, Greece was duly promised Thessaly and Epirus. But till Mr. Gladstone came into office in 1880 the promise remained unfulfilled. Then Thessaly was handed over in part payment, and now Greece demands Epirus shall be given too. For this her people are armed to the teeth and her little fleet is anchored in the Bay of Salamis, defiantly waiting the arrival of the united squadrons of the Great Powers. Of course there can be only one end to the unequal conflict. Greece must submit, but the necessity, whilst admitted, may be not the less deplored. Mr. Bradlaugh, sitting clothed and in his right place below the gangway, watched this afternoon with curious interest Mr. Gladstone and the other newly-elected members taking their seats. In other circumstances he would have been with them, and we should have had the day's doings diversified by another" Bradlaugh scene." That it should to-day have been otherwise was one of the few compensa- tions for the seven months' existence of a Conserva- tive Government. There is no doubt that had the session opened with Mr. Gladstone in power and Mr. Bradlaugh had presented himself to take the oath, there would have been now, us in 1880, oppo- sition by the Conservatives. But Sir Michael Beach being still leader of the House when Mr. Bradlaugh came up, the Speaker's inteiposition was accepted without a struggle, and the Bradlaugh incident closed. It is well, in reflecting upon the brief exist- ence of a Conservative Ministry, to remember small mercies. The acceptance of the Lord Chancellorship by Sir Farrer Herschel involves a considerable pecuniary sacrifice. The salary is £lO,OOO a year, and it is understood that in late years Sir Farrer Herschel's professional receipts have more nearly reached £20,000. But there are compensations, since the Lord Chancellor receives for life a retiring pension of £5,000 a year. The most conspicuous instance of sacrificing monetary position for official rank is to be found in the case of Mr. Horace Davey. Mr. Davey has for many years been receiving an income of considerably over £20,000 a year. As Solicitor- General he gets £6,000 and a knighthood with no retiring pension. There are fees which probably bring the official income up to £9,000 a year. Still a man who has, for some time, been earning, according to some accounts, -530,000 a year, may think himself privileged to accept a fourth of that salary. Mr. Davey is a most indefatigable worker. One of his associates told me that he thinks nothing, when in an import- ant case, of working right off twenty-four hours at a stretch without taking sleep. Sir Richard Web- ster, the late attorney-general in the Conservative Government, is also a tremendous worker, his lamp burning far into the night when he has any special case on. Sir Richard attributes his immunity from illness, in spite of his regular condition of overwork, to the fact that he is a teetotaller. The Nike case continues to be the absorbing topic of conversation wherever two or three are gathered together at the dinner table. There are still some who stand by the co-respondent, who is, I hear, daily in receipt of sympathetic letters. But I am bound to say that I have not met any of that way of thinking. Sir Charles's failure to go into the witness box and deny Mrs. Crawford's statement on oath is a circumstance beyond which most people decline to look. I believe that in this matter Sir Charles weakly allowed himself to be misled by his counsel. tip to the time he entered court he was determined to carry out the course announced by him i in his letter to his con- stituents, and, going into the witness box, deny the whole story. In failing to do that he deferred to the judgment of Sir Henry James and Mr. Charles Russell, which from a legal point of view is per- fectly defensible. The judge more than once, in a. marked manner, declared that there was no evi- dence against Sir Charles Dilke. In ordinary cases that would of course have sufficed. The highest authority having declared that there was no evi- dence against the defendant, what h ad he to combat? But this was not an ordinary case, and public senti- ment is undoubtedly right in discerning the neces- sity of a sworn denial from Sir Charles Mike. The effect of the trial as it stands ostracises Sir Charles Dilke from public life, at least for the pre- sent. I have good reason to believe that before the trial Mr. Gladstone was desirous and prepared to make provision for Sir Charles in the Cabinet. I know that Sir Charles expected to return to his old place. But since Friday he has received no com- munication from Mr. Gladstone. and will certainly not be a member of the present Government. What course he will adopt is not yet decided upon in spits of much circumstantial gossip printed on the .sub- Net. He has two courses open to him. One is to leave the country on an extended tour of travel, hoping that when he comes back the painful im- pression created by the case will have worn off. He objects to this on the score that it would look as if he were running away. The other course is to remain in town and attend to his duties as a pri- vate member as sedulously as if nothing had hap- pened. Mr. Chamberlain urges this latter course, but Sir Charles, as I have said, has not yet decided. The story about Mr. Chamberlain abandoning Sir Charles when he found he would not go into the box is an impudent fabrication. The two men are as inseparable as ever:

- There is a good story, which has the advantage of being true, circulated in connection with a well- known man of business in London. After the fashion of the day he proposed to turn his extensive business into a joint stock concern, and issued an attractive prospect i us, n which, amongst other an- nouncements, was one to the effect that an eminent firm of accountants had examined his books and were able to testify that for many years past his profits

had been over thirty per cent. A copy of the pros- pectus was inadvertently addressed to one of the Income-tax Commissioners in the district where the business was carried on. Ile turned up Mr. A.'s income-tax returns for the number of years the aaditor's statement covered, and found that it was greatly at variance with that glowing description. The Commissioner, feeling bound to accept the tes- timony of so eminent a firm, sat down quickly, and made out a claim for income-tax unpaid which reached a startling amount. This was sent in to the enterprising merchant, who must either pay up his income-tax or declare that his prospectus has been fraudulently issued. I have seen this year a repetition of what was a novelty a couple of seasons ago. At Chrestie's, and perhaps one or two of the very best auction - rooms, I have seen ladies sitting at the green table —it looked rather like Homburg or Monaco—and bidding and buying, of course, the lots on sale would be jewels or old lace or pieces of worked silk. A few years ago this would have been almost an imposssibility. Brokers made a ring that no one cared to break through. Their services were a kind of black mail—l mean, of course, for small purchases— levied inexorably. Some gentlemen broke the ring and ladies have rushed in. I hope the custom will spread, and that the tyranny of dealers over auctions will finally be over-thrown.
Tettero to the editor.

COMMUNISM. Sir,—lf " Jaques " had wed the word competition in his description of Communism, he could not well have put his case better. It is of the very essence of the present state of society to preserve both the capable and incapable alike; both extremes of society testify to this truth in a remarkable manner; whereas scientific Communism will recognise in the clearest possible manner the absolute necessity of producing and reproducing the most "capable," and the adaptation of the law of (haphazard) "natural selection," to that of scientific selection. Thus "the great natural law of evolu- tion " will "assert" "human progress" in a pre-eminent degree by removing the terrible evils that now afflict society to such a degree that the wave of progress is often hurled back, and men of little minds lose heart in the struggle to reach the happy shore. Mankind bears a close resemblance to plants; place them under right conditions, and they both flourish and prosper, whereas under bad conditions • both have to struggle for an existence. " Jaques' " ideal of commonwealth is evidently one of his own creation; cer- tainly 'tis not that of the student of Communism. " Jaques' " ideas of the incentives to labour and its rewards are mixed with the present ideas of society, where each seeks his own advantage in utter disregard of his fellow men; and he imagines that the old leaven of competition will be put into the new bottle of co-operation—that the old process of fermentation will exist under totelly new conditions. Tie true that the greater as well as the least will be grati- fied in having all their wants supplied, but that does not mean that each will possess their " wants" in the same degree. For example, two persons even in the present con- ditions of life are seated at the same table; one eats and drinks twice the amount of the other, and both are " amply " gratified. It does not follow that he who eats the most does the least work, and even if it did the small eater might require a much larger share of other pleasures, and thus the balance might be tolerably even in the end. "Incentive" will naturally vary under different condi- tions. At present, each aims to secure as much wealth as he can, on account of the insecure conditions of existing society, for we know not what a day may bring forth, be- cause all is chaos, whereas Communism will, bring about Cosmos; ergo, the "incentive" to grow rich will have no place in the individual mind, for the reason that a surplus would possess no value to its owner. Education would be free; work would become a plea- sure; recreation would be within the reach of all, because each would sea his own in all men's good. Education and culture level all class distinctions; and what would be con- sidered perfectly natural under Communism would be quite out of pie in competitive society. Natural and unnatural are relative terms, and cannot be taken as absolute under two different social systems. Warrington, Feb. 19, 1886.

div.head: W. H. CHAPMAN.
div.p: W. H. CHAPMAN.
"FORCE NO REMEDY."

Sir,—What an abundance of beautiful disquisition on morality and the conduct of man has been called forth by the London riots. We have been told with endless itera- tion of the wickedness of those who have broken the public peace, of the sacred rights of property which have been violated, and of the nobility of the workman who would rather starve himself and see his family starve than touch a farthing's worth of that wealth which he and his class have mostly created but which others enjoy; and a re- markable number of these excellent homilies seem to be written to point the moral of the most respectable maxim "Force is no remedy." This, no doubt, is all very proper and orthodox, but here, as in so many other cases, truth is heterodox and a great disregarder of the rules of propriety. So far from force being no remedy, truth compels one to say in regard to political and social ills that force seems to be the universal and only effectual remedy. It is nearly imposAble to point to any great beneficial change in the political or social conditions of a people which has not been the product of more or less force, and generally more than less. The regeneration of France, the unification of Italy and Germany, the working out of the aspirations of the people of Hungary, and we may now add of Bulgaria are all due to force, and that of a very drastic kind. To come to our own country, the extorting of Magna Charts from King John, the revolution through which Charles I. lost his head, and that of 1688 which sent another Stuart to the right-about, have always been regarded as having had something to do with the securing and maintaining of our " boasted !Reales," and yet in these instances it was found that the grand panacea for social and political ills was force, pure, and unadulterated. In the present century the passing of the great Reform Bill was materially facili- tated by certain popular outbreaks; the Hyde Park riot had something to do with the enactment of that ot 1868; and the latent physical powers of the unenfranchised was an unanswerable argument in favour of the most recent ex- tension of the franchise. Of Catholic emancipation the Duke of Wellington said "We have to choose between emancipation and rebellion, and I prefer the former as the less evil of the two." The Protestant Church in Ireland was disestablished, as has been truly said, "because the Fenians I blew down a gaol in Clerkenwell, and burst open a police- van in Manchester." To the methods of the Land League —and no one will say that force was not one of these methods are due the Irish Land Acts; and should Home Rule be granted it will be a result of similar methods of winning political priveleges. This maxim if "force no remedy" is oftenest used im connection with the Irish ques- tion, yet it is a curious fact that no matter bow that ques- tion may be settled, whether by rigid and persistent repres- sion or the granting of the Irish demands, the settlement will have been wrought out by force, in the one case by the bayonets and buckshot of soldiery and police, and in the other by the shooting and stabbing of obnoxious indivi- duals, the maiming of cattle, and boycotting and terrorism in general. It is quite clear then that this "force no remedy" doctrine has no validity about it. It ought to be amended and expressed in such terms as these "Insuffi- cient force is no remedy." Force which was inadequate to accomplish the purpose of those who used it hat often made matters worse for them, but not otherwise. Perhaps our writers of homilies would not care for the amended doctrine even if nearer the truth.

div.head: SOCIALISM.
div.p: SOCIALISM.

Sir,—l have no intention of interfering with the discus- sion on "Social equality " now going on in your columns. Mr. Chapman will, no doubt, be able to pulverize and sweep away every atom of argument "Jaques" may bring to bear on the subject, and when this feat has been accom- plished the question will still remain, what are we to do with our struggling poor? The never-ending dispute as to the exact meaning of the words landlord and capitalist may, I think, now be brought to a close, and in its place be substi- tuted a desire to take hold of the Social question in some practical form. I take it that the word "Socialism" stands for a principle. Around it gathers all that tends towards uniting the human family in one grand and noble brother- hood. When a man becomes unsociable, he becomes an out- cast of society—one to be avoided on account of special and peculiar failings. The new Socialism would say, "No, no Man shall be an outcast. Is he a weak and erring brother? Then search and find out the reason, for surely there is one, ta lett h e rea,e remedynworking, tim esentiment!" h! I each fancy applied, s a membersmo same that h af for oner tlle society m "thistauy be i s a gooept d." "Mere Socialism; not Socialism means a mob meeting in Trafalgar- square, spreading out thence over the West End of London, breaking into jewellers' shops, smashing club windows, Sic.— this is what Socialism means, and we will have none of it." Well, Mr. Editor, neither is this my Socialism, and if I am further told that Socialism means "taking from the rich to give to the poor," I still disown it. But what then is saying; mu Socialism? The public have a right to ask this question, and the answer must not be given by mob orators. William Morris, keeping the good time in view, sings:— Then all neine and all thint shall be ours, And no more shall any man crave, For riches that serve for nothing, But to fetter a friend or a slave." Oh, some one will say, " that's beautiful, but mere senti- ment, and differing very little from Mr. Chapman'e Utopian views." The general impression is that the lines I have quoted involve the doing away with the competitive spirit that at present exists in man, and would reduce him to such an apathetic and careless state as would in the long run end in his total and complete demoralization. Of the truth of this I am not clear, the emulative spirit in man is co-exis- tent with the law of evolution, and must, I think, although Conentuniam *aro adopted, carry men upward and onward, and so prevent his drifting back into his primitive state. A very aoe statistician, Mr. (Wren, has recently put forth some very remarkable statements, tending to prove that working-men " have got to themselves nearly the whole product of the aggregate industry of the country," and that they, the workmen, are now receiving from 30 to 100 per cent, more money wages for .20 per cent. less work." Such a statement coming from so high an authority is, naturally, hailed with glee by those whose interest it is to keep up the present very unsatisfactory state of things. Can it be truly said that the working-man receives his share of the profits of his labour, when Mr. Malhall points out that "the I

div.head: JAQUES.
div.p: JAQUES.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY, 20, 1886.

higher classes, who number only 222,000 families, possess' wealth of the value of £5,728,000,000 ; the middle classes, who number 1.824,000 families' possess £1,834,000,000; the working classes, who number 4,629,100 families, possess only £398,000,000." I ask are we, the workmen, to be told that we are receiving our share when the non-producing classes possess a total of £7,562,000,000 to £398,000,000 possessed by the working classes? In ten years' time 74 , capitalists died worth £48,600,000. In 1875 eight capitalistsl died in Liverpool worth £4,650,000. In the metropolis in 184'9 71 persons died of starvation ; in 1882 54 died of star- vation; la 1883 58 died of starvation! Here we have a moral quite strong enough to point out the road to Socialism. People are starving for want of work, those who are in work ind the tension of life almost too heavy to bear. What is the remedy? The Socialist sings again in cur ear— "l tell you this for a wonder, That no man then *hall be glad Of his fellow's fall and mb.hap ' ' To snatch at the work he had."

I say, do not make any attempt at pillage, at robbery, for however we twist terms, or however we chop logic, we shall fail if we make any attempt at upsetting the laws tjaat at present govern society by any anarchical move- ment. Our remedy lies in a steady and persevering study of politics. Let us find out what it is that is eating away the ' result of our toil. When a man finds out that near upon 16s oat of every sovereign that he earns goes towards keeping Royalty, aristocracy, religion, army, and navy he may possibly conclude that it is high time for him to put the question to himself, "What do I gain by supporting either Liberal or Tory? Had I not better formulate a series of questions bearing upon my immediate welfare, question the candidate, and according to his answer be guided?" But it is not sufficient to elect a representative. and leave him unquestioned to act and vote -as he may please in Parliament ; he must be watched. In the old time the rich man elected the rich man to represent him, and he knew his interests were safe; to-day the rich man is sent to represent rich and poor alike. We are now hoping for laws that will create outlets for fortunes that grow out of toil. We are earnestly seeking that the land shall bear and support its due share of workers, and not drive them into the town to add to the already congested state of the labour market, and to put a stop to a state of things where- by wealth accumulates and men decay. CLIFFORD DIX. February 15th, 1888.
hAT FST NEWS.
The Earl and Countess of Aberdeen left London last evening for Dublin Mr. W. E. Forster, M.P., is again improving, but he is stilt far from St to attend to his duties in Parliament.
The New South Wales Ministry has resigned. Sir Patrick Jennings has been charged with the formation of a new Cabinet.

The illness of the Earl of Winchelsea has assumed a serious character. A consultation of physicians took place on Friday. The death, from bronchitis, is announced of Mr. Fredk. Balsir Chatterton, who for many years has been associated with Drury-lane Theatre. The Duke of Edinburgh will arrive at Portsmouth to-day from London, and will sail in the afternoon to take com- mand of the Mediterranean Squadron. The German Government are preparing a workmen's old age insurance bill, which will provide for the payment of pensions to operatives who are past the power of work- ing. On Thursday night, almost without warning, snow began to fall heavily over the northern and eastern districts of Scotland. Agricultural and fishing operations are again at a standstill.

A Philadelphia correspondent telegraphs that Mr. John B. Gough, whose death was prematurely announced a few days ago, at the time when he was struck down by paralysis, died yesterday. WATERLOO Cu.—The meet on Friday morning was at Hill House, the weather again being fine but very cold. In the deciding course for the Waterloo Cup Miss Gleudyne beat Penelope 11., and won the cup (£500.)

THE PIMLICO POISONING CASE. At Westminster, London, on Friday, before Mr. Partridge, Mrs. Adelaide Bartlett, aged 30, and the Rev. Geo. Dyson, aged 27, were placed in the dock together and charged—the former with the murder of her husband, Edwin Thomas Bartlett, and the latter with being an accessory before the fact. The court was densely crowded, and the case was gone into at some hngth.

The Liverpool magistrates, on Tharsday, committed for trial the thirteen boys charged with mutiny on board a re- formatory ship. The evidence showed a firm determina- tion on the part of some of the lads to do grievous harm to the officers.

BREACH OF PROMISR.—A breach of promise of marriage case, brought by Miss Katerino Corio against Mr. Ernest Salmon, son of a Brighton chemist, came before Mr. Justice Hawkins at the Sussex Assizes on Wednesday, and ended in the plaintiff being awarded .4200. SOUTHPORT AND CHRSHIRE LINEIS.—The half-yearly re- port of the directors of the Southport and Cheshire Lines Extension Company says that the earnings of the railway for the past.half year give:£l7 per mile per week, as against £l4 for the previous six months. The directors consider that the company is suffering from the depression which has affected all other railways. The Cheshire Lines Committee have completed the necessary works, and there is now ac- commodation for dealing in all descriptions of traffic at all places.

Grioss LIBIL Blf A GENTLEMLIC—SEVERE) SENTENCE.— At Winchester Assizes, on Tuesday, Vivian Arthur Webber, artist, described as a gentleman, pleaded guilty to uttering a false and malicious libel on some ladies named Hasty.at Hyde. —Mr. Justice Stephen said he had read the entire history of the case, which dated back to August, 1884, in which gross imputations were made on the lady and her daughter. The prisoner was a wilful and malicious liar, and his lord- ship regretted he could not inflict bard labour. He would sentence him, however, to four months' imprisonment, with every form of indignation such as thieves and rogues suf. !ered, to pay a fine of £l5O, and to find sureties for Ave years.

132111011 S FIRES.—A very destructive fire broke out on Saturday afternoon in the block of buildings belonging to Messrs. J. B. Baldwin and Co., oil and varnish manufactu- rers, of Spread Eagle Wharf, Sutton. The damage is esti- mated at £32,000.—0n Sunday, a fire occurred in Mr. J. Tattersall's flannel manufactory, at Wardle, near Rochdale. The main five-storey building was totally destroyed. The weaving shed and other portions of the mill were saved. The damage is estimated at £8,000.--A great tire, the second within eight days, occurred at the esparto sheds at Car- diff on Saturday night. Damage to the amount of £lO,OOO or £12,000 was done. There is a suspicion of in- cendiarism.—A large warehouse in Houndsditch. London, stored principally with a valuable stock of Japanese goods ' and fancy articles, was destreyed by fire on Monday. The premises are occupied by Messrs. Anton Brander and CO. The damage is estimated at £25,000.

div.head: MILITARY ORGANISATION IN EGYPT.
div.p: MILITARY ORGANISATION IN EGYPT.

Cento, FRlDAY.—Mukhtar Pasha has submitted to the Khedive and Sir Henry Wolff a memorandum relating to the plan for the pacification of the Soudan and for the re- organisation of the Egyptian army, which he presented at the third Conference on the 27th ult. It is understood that the memorandum strongly recommends the re-occupation ot Dongola as a strategical necessity, that place forming the only efficacious barrier between Egypt and the insur- gent tribes.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met at 4 o'clock.

The Lord CIUNCELLOR presented two bills for the con- solidation and amendment of lunacy laws.—Lord CRAx- BROOK gave notice for Monday to ask for information res- pecting boycotting and other crimes in Ireland.—The House then adjourned.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The HOll3O met at 4 o'clock.

NamEs.—Mr. LABOUCHERE gave notice that on that day fortnight he should move his resolution with respect to the hereditary character of the Legislature.—Dr. CAMERON gave notice on going into committee of supply he should move that the Church of Scotland ought to be disestablished and disendowed.

QUESTIONS.—Mr. CHILDERS replying to Mr. J. Stuart, said he could not then state the intentions of the Govern- ment as te the reform of the municipal govern- ment of London. • Mr. GLADSTONR, replying to Sir M. Beach, said it was intended to pro- pose Mr. Courtney as Chairman of Committees.—Mr. Gladstone, replying to Sir E. Birkbeck, said he could not make any statement as to the advisability of employing workmen, who were at present out of employ, in order to carry out works for the formation of harbours of re- fuge. SUPPLY.— On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. HEALY called attention to the eviction of a widow named Ann Shaw from her freehold in the county of Monaghan, and moved a resolution.—Mr. J. MORLEY (Irish Secretary) said the matter in question was now before a court of inquiry, and therefore he could express no opinion on the subject until the report was presented.— The resolution was withdrawn.—Mr. GLADSTONE afterwards moved that Mr. Courtney take the chair, and that gentle- man took the chair. Several votes were agreed to. On the vote for £3OO for Dover Harbour, Sir G. Balfour and Sir R. Peel protested against the vote. They wished to know whether voting this small sum would commit the House to the expenditure .of over seven hundred thousand pounds for enlarging the harbour. Sir H. Holland and Mr. Gladstone intimated that the vote would not have that effect.

div.head: SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL BILL.

This bill will be opposed by the Mersey Docks and Har- bour Board, the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany, and the Corporation of Liverpool. These bodies were the principal opponents of the bill which authorises the carrying out of the undertaing.

The following letter has appeared in the Times : Sir,—l hare read with great satisfaction the speech of Lord Salisbury in reply to-the deputation from t'ne unem- ployed, and as one portion has special reference to a matter whichileepLy concerns the prosperity of this district, and with it the labour question 4 trust you will allow me space for a few remarks upon a bill which is now before Parliament. I refer to the Manchester Ship Canal Additional Powers Bill, asking for Dowers to pay interest during construc- tion.

There may be a naisconception placed upon your able leader were it not pointed out that the Regent's Canal Com- pany, with the support of Lord Salisbury and Mr. Chamber- lain as President of the Board of Trade, obtaiaed last session powers to pay interest, notwithstanding the strong vested interests which had to be contended against, and it is not unlikely that opposition to our bill may come from tho-e who consider their interests are affected, but who have al- ready, during the construction of their own works, paid, and are now paying, interest themselves, although some leading railway directors have promised us their generous support. In our case we cannot complete our works or earn revenue from them for a period estimated at four years, during which time it will be necessary to outlayat least £8,000.000, and it is as monstrous to ask investors to lend their money without return for this period as it would be to ask for the -materials and labour on credit.

All we want is that the works when completed by us should coat us the same price as though they had been con- structed by a third party and handed ever on completion to us at a net cost,which of courre would include interest._

No great undertaking in the world has been carried out successfully over a period of years without similar pay- ments, nor is there in any country, excepting ours, a neces- sity to go to the Legislature to obtain the right, from which it may be assumed that it is`tonly Englishmen who do not know their own business.

Our shareholders, already thousands in number, ask unanimously for the powers, which, if granted, will mean the continuous employment of many thousands of labourers and artizans, and new investors are ready to join us in our great national undertaking if Parliament acts upon the pre- cedent of last year. This is a question far above party, and I trust that all classes of politicians will unite to help us to proceed with a work which will do so mach to solve the great labour problem and to assist the great industries of the country. • Yours faithfully, DANIEL ADAMSON, Chairman of the Manchester Ship Canal Company. Manchester.
• On Wednesday the Glasgow police apprehended Thomas Lee. aged 62, colliery manager, at Bedlington, Northumber- land, on a charge of fraud. Lee was about to proceed to America. _

Tno DEPRESSED TRADE COMMISSION.—The Royal Com- mission on the Depression of Trade and Industry held another meeting on Thursday at Richmond Terrace, White- hall. the Earl of Iddesleigh presiding. All the members were present. Evidence was given of the depression in tex- tile fabric industries, particularly in regard to cotton goods. 'VULCAN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SatooL.—lfl aid of the funds of this school a very enjoyable gathering was held in the dining-room of the Vulcan Foundry on Wednesday evening. The room had been kindly lent for the occasion, by Mr. E. Brettelle manager of the foundry. The gather- ing took the form Of a vocal and instrumental concert by a number of friends from Bolton, and it proved a deserved success in every respect. The attendance was large, and the various selections were highly appreciated. The Instrumen- tal music was supplied by the string band connected with the Congregational Sunday School, in St. George's-road, Bolton, and the vocalists were members of the choir con- nected with St. George's-road Congregational Church. Mr. John Ihornley, organist of the Wesleyan Chapel, Fletcher- street, Bolton, and Mr. John Tayler, of Bolton, officiated as reader.

Adam-street, Strand, London. iV•IJ TEz Socialista are just now receiving more than, ordinary altention ; some of them are ' being prosecutedifor their share in the riots whiCh took place in London last week; and we may safely assume that when they come to defend themselves they will make the most of the opportunity which will be afforded ' them of promulgating their views. But there are Socialists, and Socialias, and to prevent , confusion it is needful to distinguish and de- fine. it has always been considered a 'good sort of stick to beat a Radical dog with to , say "he is a Sce.ialist." There are very . many Radicals, however, who are not So- cialists, although there are few Socialists who are not Radicals. In one Sense, all Refor- mers are Socialists, as Mr. CIiA2ISERLAIN not t long since aptly pointed out in a vigorous pas- sage of one of his best speeches. Our poor-law system ia based upon Socialism; there is Socialism in the Artizans' Dwellings Act, in the Libraries Acts, in the Fasttory Acts, in the - Mines Regulation and Employers' Liability Acts, and in others that might be named. This is the kind of State Socialism which ex- perience has approved, which is for the most part justified by results, and which, it is be- lieved, warrants new experiments in the direc- tion of "three acres and a cow." Mr. BRAD- LAUGH, like Mr. (.;HAMBERLA3N, has often had hurled at his head the charge of being a Socialist ; but he repudiates the term, and has publiely opposed Mr. H. M. HYNDMAN, • the chief priest of present-clay Socialists. The - strict Socialist believes, as the Owenites did, that the basis of society is fundamentally wrong; that property, should be held not by individuals, but by the State; and that society is to be regenerated, by getting rid of that fierce competition in which the weak so fre- quently go to the wall. The theory is very : pretty as a theory, but as human nature is constituted it is impossible to reduce it to t, practice: and we hold, therefore, that the Socialists proper in so far as they are leading , people astray with false hopes are do- ing a great deal more harm than good. Not being able to gain converts by appeals to reason, the Socialists of the Democratic, Federation have begun to try what appeals to brute force will do. They succeeded last week, but it was by an acci- dent as it were; they made use of a gather- ing which was not their own, and the police being unprepared for a disturbance, the roughs of London—not the respectable un- employed—had a day of window smashing and looting at the West End. Speaking for ourselves, we have no fear that : the Gospel of Grab, as it is preached by leaders of the Democratic Federation, will make headway amongst the masses of the toilers of this country. They are, as a body, too conscientious to entertain proposals for - plundering capitalists; and they have sense enough to see that, bad as things may be,. society is not to be mended by the app:ica- tion of brand new springs of action.whicle are not in harmony with the nature and conatitu- tion of man. We do not wish to suggest that the Socialists are wrong in all 'chat they 3dvo- - ; far from it, for we believe that what is good, in their programme is Radicalism pure and simple; it is what is bad in their creed that is peculiarly their own. Take, the , question of the land ; there are many refor- mers who. are not Socialists who believe in. Land Nationalisation ; but. they do not pro- pose, as leading Socialists do, that the State • shall appropriate land "with or without come- pensation In "Socialism made plain, be. ing the social and political manifesto of the, Democratic Federation," we are tcld with, re— ference to the land that—" The handful of' marauders who now hold possession have a.el can have no right, save brute force, against: the tens of millions whom they wrong.' A sweeping statement like this applies of conraa with as much, or as little, force to the woak- ineeman who has perchased the freehold; on which his house stands, as to the lord, oT the many acres which have come, to him by in- heritance. There is no mistaking language of this kind; these Social Democrat's affect to believe that the State tvond be quite justi- fied in taking,: possession of the land without giving the present owners one penny "for value received." Having gobbled up theland, there need be no hesitation about seizing all that is on it, and, accordingly, we find among the "stepping stories to a hanpier period,' a proposal fter the "State appropriation of Railways, wi:th or without compensation." But surely it ,would be more appeopriate to, speak of v.zleolesale theft of this kind as a "stepping stone"! to the gallows. Two years since, during the last great strike in East Laneashire, some of the leaders of the Democratic Federation paid a visit to Black- burn. It is a point with thera.to stir up strife amongst the 'discontented; but in this, in- stance they we're not successful. The opera- tives on strike,, certainly relished denuncia- tions of mataufzacturers, but when it came to a question of Cite State taking possession of everything " with or without compensation," they showed n o sign—they looked on these preachers of view fangled doctrines as crazy theorists, and. well they might. QucstioneaP as to how -.they proposed to recoestitute society, some of the leaders explained that , they woucl get rid altogether of private pro- perty; the State would have a right, without 1 payment, to, take possession of everything, mills, mines?, forges, factories, snd works of every kind toe work them for the sole benefit of the peog)le. Was there ever, outside bedlam, such a mad proposal as that society should cut it own throat in order to secure it own salvaition.? We have heard less of

One of the stones fell upon the head of a child belonging to Henry Lee, fireman on the railway, and killed it.

LYMM. SUDDEN DRATIL—A young woman, daughter of Joho Collins, platelayer on the L. and N.-W. Railway, did veil suddenly at Heatley on Saturday. CONSERVATIVE CLUB.—On Monday evening the members of the Lymm Conservative Club played their third annual billiard match with the members of the Sale Conservative Club, on the tables of the latter. The game was an enjer able one, Lymm being victorious. REDUCTIONS OF RENC—Mr. G. C. Dewhuret, of Lyming has we understand permanently • reduced the rents of hie tenants 10 per cent, owing to the depression of agriculture t and the low prices realised for farm stock. One nr two landowners in the neighbourhood have followed the eX• ample and made reductions in rent. ENTERTAINMENT.—On Monday evening an entertainment was given in the concert room of the Plough Hotel by the members of the "Old Kentucky Minstrels." There was s good attendance. The programme consisted of topical songs' choruses, jokes, solos, bone solo, negro farce, &c., and Corr eluded with sangs in character, and a sleight of hand per- formance. THE UNEMPLOYED.—In order to alleviate as far as Poe- sible the distress in Lymm, owing to shortness of work, free meals are being given to poor children on Tuesday arid Thursday in each week at the Coffee Tavern. On ' average about 50 children partake of the meal. The funds are raised by voluntary subscriptions amongst the residents in the neighbourhood. ZION INDEPENDENT METHODIST CHAPEL.-OTI MORdAY • evening the annual Sunday School tea party in connection with the above place of worship was held, when about 100 persons sat down to tea. Afterwards a public meeting and entertainment were held. Mr. James Dodds occupied the chair, and the report of the committee, which was read bi the secretary, was considered very satisfactory, the report showing an increase of 30 scholars and 11 teachers during the past year. The entertainment which followed consisted of songs, and recitations, &c., by the scholars and friends, The choir, under the leadership of Mr. Henry Daniels, ac• companied by Mr. Alfred Long, rendered a choice selec• tion of hymns, &c. Mr. E. Brown and Mr. J. Knowles de' livered short and appropriate speeches.
